en: In Zen practice, the primary aim is the realization of one's nature; in the study of the scriptures, the emphasis is on illuminating the mind.
In the single gate of Buddha-recitation (*nien-fo*), both Zen and the teachings proceed in unison, for this is the natural principle of the Way.

It is not merely empty words that the Great Master [Yung-ming Yen-shou] now synthesizes all myriad practices within the Samadhi of Buddha-recitation and initiates all virtues with the precept against taking life. At first, it was said that adhering to principle while abandoning phenomena would lead to error.
There is the calamity of falling into emptiness for those who cling to practice while remaining deluded regarding principle; yet even so, there remains the benefit of rebirth in the Pure Land.

This is a path that Zen practitioners may descend to reach, and those of the Teaching school may strive upward to attain. It serves to refine those among the followers of Zen and the Teaching who harbor defects, directly pointing to the way back to the source in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, it is said that the social customs of the age have become thin and corrupt, with people vying for the frivolous and the ornate to an extreme.
Driven by the cravings of the mouth and belly, one exhausts every delicacy of land and water;
yet, possessing no sense of shame and lacking the heart of compassion, one calls oneself a Confucian while betraying the transformative influence of benevolence and nurturance.

To restrain others from killing and to encourage the release of living beings is the means by which one embodies the Great Compassion of all Buddhas above and fulfills the profound love of sentient beings below. Alas! These are the words of Jingci.
How magnificent! Were it not for one whose Chan and doctrinal teachings are perfectly clear, whose benevolence and compassion are vast and great, how could we have reached this point?

To look up and praise the Great Master—whom the world calls an Ancient Buddha—is truly fitting. He may indeed be called a precious torch in the dark alleys and a compassionate vessel across the sea of suffering.
Among the bookstalls of Luoyang, who else in the wild fields could have requested me to consult the facts of his life and achieve the labor of carving these woodblocks? I, [Name], have done so.
Though I have the honor of studying Chan, I am not yet fully conversant with the Pure Land; nevertheless, I have roughly recorded what I have examined and appended it to this book.
It is my hope that those who see or hear of it may all find encouragement to practice, so that both monastics and laypeople alike may partake in its benefit and joy. Thus it is said.

Written on the Buddha’s Birthday in the first month of summer in the *guichou* year of the Kwanmu era, respectfully appended by the monk Sōyū of Shiji-san in Sanzan Province to the *Biography of Master Yongjue*.
The Weilun Lu states: After the Chan Master had shaved his head, he followed his dharma-elder, Master Boshan, for three years following the latter’s passing.
In the inscription for his stupa, it mentions that after the Master’s passing, [the author] relied upon his fellow disciple, Chan Master Wuyi of Boshan, for three years and received full ordination.
Subsequently, he took leave to return to Min to dwell in the mountains; as his boat crossed the Jian River, he encountered [the following].
He heard the Sangha chanting the *Lotus Sūtra*: "At one time, they coughed and simultaneously snapped their fingers;

these two sounds reached throughout the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions. Upon hearing this, he attained vast and great enlightenment, thoroughly penetrating the point of Shouchang’s application [of the Dharma].
(And so forth. When the Master reached the age of fifty-six, he went to visit Great Master Wengu at Baoshan; upon seeing him once, [he was enlightened].
Through a profound spiritual affinity, he was earnestly encouraged to leave the secular world, which was the tradition passed down from Yunqi;
the next year, he was granted the *Jieben* (Precepts Manual) and accepted an invitation to Mount Gu.

He still resided as a hermitage master for another two years before opening the Dharma at Kaiyuan Temple in Quanzhou, where the incense in his breast was finally offered by the Elder Wuming. The Master said: "Chan fundamentally derives from Shouchang (who first resided at Baofang...)"

Later, he resided at Zhuchi; his *Jieben* (Precepts Manual) and *Zhenji* (True Stillness) cannot be falsely attributed to others. Subsequently, he propagated the Dharma at Zhenji in Hangzhou and at Baoshan in Yan.
Later, he returned to Gushan, where he reconstructed the temple buildings and extensively expounded the teachings of his school.
Throughout the realm, all revered him as the "Ancient Buddha. His recorded sayings from three assemblies and various writings total twenty works.
In more than eighty fascicles (the details of which are fully contained in the *Record of the Venerable Layman Lin Hanzhai’s Conduct*).
Preface to the *Essential Words of Jingci*:
What is Jingci? It is the name of a hermitage bestowed by the Great Master Wengu. As for why the hermitage was named Jingci:

What is meant by "releasing life through mindfulness of the Buddha"? That which is sought through releasing life through mindfulness of the Buddha is the restoration of the mind’s original purity and original compassion. Indeed, the fundamental mind is vast and eternally pure;

it is only when sentient beings are deluded regarding this fundamental state that they perceive phenomena as being external to the mind—thus, the eyes are defiled by forms, the ears by sounds, and the nose by fragrances.
The tongue is defiled by flavors, the body by tactile sensations, and the mind by mental phenomena; they flow outward in restlessness, unable to return to themselves.

From this, karma is produced and transgressions are committed, leading to eternal sinking in the region of the five turbidities with no prospect of escape. Our Buddha, taking pity on them, has therefore taught the Dharma for treating these defilements and returning to purity.
Although the dispositions of sentient beings are not uniform and the teachings likewise differ, the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha [is universal].

The most essential point among these single gates is the single-minded recitation of the Buddha’s name with undivided intent. When the six sense faculties are all brought under control and pure mindfulness continues without interruption,
then the eyes will not be defiled by forms, the ears will not be defiled by sounds, the nose will not be defiled by fragrances, the tongue will not be defiled by flavors,
the body will not be defiled by tactile objects, and the mind will not be defiled by mental phenomena— even while remaining in this Sahā world.
If one has already merged within the body and is seated in the Land of Lotus, how could there be any impurity regarding future retribution?
Nevertheless, although one may practice the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection, if merit and virtue are not complete, the good fruit will be difficult to achieve.

Therefore, one must extensively cultivate various virtues to serve as auxiliary causes. Among the many virtues, compassionate conduct is foremost; and among the many forms of compassionate conduct, [the following] is paramount.

Yet, abstaining from killing and releasing captive creatures is the foremost [of virtues]. This is because among all sentient beings, there is nothing they love more than life and nothing they suffer more than death.

All who possess breath and vitality share this sentiment universally; it is only because we have become habituated to callousness that our innate compassion for those of the same substance becomes paralyzed and fails to function.
Thus, we calmly slaughter and kill without deeming it strange—how could this be the heart’s [true nature]?
It is but natural that for this reason our Buddha, with bitter words and earnest exhortation, first forbade the taking of life and widely encouraged the release of living beings.
To save what one loves most and thereby rescue what suffers most—how great is the merit that reaches all things!
In Jianzhou City, both monastics and laypeople have followed the Great Master’s teachings, being devoted to the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name and releasing living beings.
Even after so many years, I still feared that its influence might not spread widely and far;
therefore, I consulted with him, and he compiled essential passages from various texts on Pure Land and the precept against killing, entrusting them to the printing blocks.

It is my hope that the transformation of Jingci Monastery may thus overflow in inexhaustible abundance. Alas! The significance of Jingci is vast; how could it be limited merely to the recitation of the Buddha’s name?
It is simply a matter of birth. Reciting the Buddha’s name and releasing living beings can be described as "Pure Compassion," yet it cannot exhaustively encompass the full meaning of Pure Compassion.
To speak at the ultimate level: when purity reaches its limit and awakening becomes perfect, one achieves the Unsurpassed Way; this does not transcend the principle of Purity.

To extensively deliver sentient beings with compassion that extends through eternal kalpas likewise does not transcend the principle of Compassion. Indeed, the various Bodhisattvas seek the fruit of Buddhahood above, while...
To transform sentient beings below, [the Master] drew from all preceding and succeeding Mahāyāna sūtras;
these works are so voluminous they could fill ox-carts and house rafters, yet he has now encapsulated them within these two characters, leaving no essential meaning unexpressed.

How could one dare say that the Great Master’s intention in naming this was limited merely to *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha's name) and releasing living beings? You gentlemen should well comprehend this intent and expand upon it.
It may be so; nevertheless, there is yet one further phrase that even the two characters "Jingci" (Pure Compassion) cannot encompass.
I wish to explain it all for you gentlemen, but alas, my tongue is too short! Gentlemen, you must examine this with the Great Master.
Written on the third day after the Dragon Boat Festival in the Jiashu year of the Chongzhen era by the monk Yuanxian of Gushan.

Regarding the source of the Pure Land teachings:
in the past, the Buddha appeared in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition, preaching various dharmas to universally accommodate the capacities of all sentient beings;
this was nothing other than removing the defilement of habitual taints to restore my original purity. However, since the capacities [of beings] have already...

While teachings are not uniform and differ in a thousand ways, if one seeks that which is easiest for practice, most stable for entering the Way, and swiftest for attaining results, nothing compares to the single gate of the Pure Land.
What is this Pure Land? It refers to the fact that within the great void of space, lands are arrayed in manifold variety—some pure and some defiled;
when the mind of a sentient being is pure, they are born in a pure land, and when the mind is turbid, they are born in a turbid land.
If one is born in a defiled land, obstacles and afflictions deepen daily, making it difficult for wholesome dharmas to be accomplished;

if one is born in a pure land, obstacles and afflictions are gradually eliminated, making it easy for wholesome dharmas to be achieved. Therefore, those who study the Way must distinguish between the pure and the defiled.
Even within the pure lands, there are various distinctions, the most preeminent of which is the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
This world has been accomplished through the immeasurable power of the vows and the immeasurable merit of Amitābha Buddha;
thus, its meritorious adornments are so vast that they cannot be matched by any other direction. Now, to briefly outline its general features, there are twenty kinds of sublime excellence:
first, the ground is made of gold, with ponds of the seven treasures, jeweled nets, and rows of trees.
1. The railings and pavilions are all composed of the seven precious jewels. 2. Within these two lands, there is no suffering from the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
3. All beings born there are produced by transformation within lotus flowers inside ponds made of the seven precious jewels.
4. Their bodies are golden in color and fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man. 5. Their bodies emit a radiance that eclipses the sun and the moon. 6. [Their] lifespan...
1. It is immeasurable and forever free from the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death. 2. The seven requisites of clothing and food appear spontaneously according to one's wishes.
3. One’s kin are able to see the Buddha and hear him preach the wondrous Dharma. 4. One assembles together with all supreme virtuous persons in one place.
5. There is no lustful sound or female form. 6. There is no enmity, hatred, or opposition. 7. There are no demonic armies or externalists. 8. There is no duality.
14. All vehicles turn from the small toward the great; 15. the sounds of the wind, the resonance of water, and the melodies of all birds all proclaim the wondrous Dharma;
16. hundreds of thousands of celestial musical instruments constantly sound day and night; 17. they are fully endowed with supernormal powers; 18.
they are able to reach the worlds of the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas; 19. they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas; 20. as soon as they are born...
In that land, one immediately dwells on the stage of non-retrogression for twenty kalpas, and at the end of this single lifetime, one attains ultimate Buddhahood.
Since this realm possesses such extraordinary benefits for sentient beings, all beings ought to seek rebirth in that land.
For those who seek rebirth there, it cannot be achieved by any other minor merits; rather, they should exclusively uphold the name of that Buddha.
One will immediately attain rebirth there. Why is this? It is because of the power of that Buddha’s great vows.
Long ago, when that Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path, he made forty-eight vows to deliver all sentient beings. Among them was one vow which says:
"If there are sentient beings who wish to be born in my land and call upon my name even ten times, yet are not born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
Because of this vow, if one single-mindedly recites the Name without distraction, one will certainly attain rebirth there.
When that person is near the end of life, Amitābha Buddha will emit a great radiance and, together with the assembly of holy beings, appear before them, extending his hand to welcome and guide them.
In the space of a finger-snap, that person will be reborn within a sublime lotus flower in that land; as the flower opens, they shall behold [the Buddha].
The Buddha immediately expounded various sublime Dharmas for them; having heard them, they realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
From this point on, they progressed until they attained Buddhahood. All that is listed above is fully detailed in various sutras as the patriarchs propagated and upheld [the Dharma];
it is certainly not false and must be faithfully believed. However, within this there are both phenomena (*事*) and principle (*理*), and practitioners should not neglect either.

What is meant by "phenomena"? It refers to all the various phenomena of the Pure Land listed above. What is meant by "principle"? It refers to the thorough understanding that all phenomena do not transcend the single mind.

Although it is said that the Pure Land is "mind-only," this does not preclude the existence of the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), for the world is precisely what is manifested by the single mind.
Although it is said that Amitābha is one's own original nature, [it does not preclude the existence of the Buddha].
It is not precluded that there is a Master of Sukhāvatī, for the Master is precisely what is accomplished through one's own original nature (*prakṛti*).
Although he is quiescent and without birth, it is not precluded that he manifests a blazing birth; yet, while he appears to go to rebirth, he is fundamentally without birth.
Those of lofty intelligence mostly delight in discussing principles and deride actual practice, while those of middling and lower capacity mostly cling to the literal facts of events.
To act while remaining deluded and ignorant of the true principle is to be entirely unaware that there is no phenomenon outside of principle, and that phenomena are themselves within principle.

To cling to principle while abandoning phenomena leads to the calamity of falling into emptiness; yet, to cling to phenomena while being deluded about principle still carries the benefit of rebirth in the Pure Land.
How can one covet empty talk and thereby incur actual disaster?
In the practice of Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti*), right faith is the primary requirement for cultivating this dharma-gate.

It is through this faith that one may enter the path of the Buddhas of the three periods, the great Bodhisattvas, and the successive patriarchs; without this faith, one will remain hesitant and indecisive.

If one’s resolve is vacillating and lacks sincerity, then regardless of whether one is unwilling to practice, or even if one is willing to practice, if the effort is intermittent—appearing and disappearing, starting and stopping—one will lack the power to "drive a nail through iron" and the intent to "shoot arrows that pierce stone.
How, then, could such a person accomplish this rare and sublime merit? Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Faith is the source of the Path."
The Mother of Merit: Faith can nurture all roots of goodness; faith can transcend the paths of the māras; faith can enable one to enter samādhi. What is meant by faith?
It is the awakening to the true source and deep belief in the reality-mark (dharmatā). If one is not yet able to do so, one must first faithfully believe the words of the Buddha.
In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, the Buddhas of the six directions all extend their broad and long [tongues]...
The Tathāgata’s tongue now exhorts you to have faith in this sutra. This is because we ordinary beings possess darkened minds and inferior faculties;

bound by our immediate habits, we are unable to know distant and vast realms or profound and subtle states. Upon encountering extraordinary events, we immediately harbor doubts and do not dare to believe.
Therefore, ordinary beings should simply and resolutely follow the Buddha’s words. The Buddha, with his heart of great compassion and great...
With a mind of wisdom, one speaks truthful words, entirely free from falsehood or deception. If one does not believe the words of the Buddha, what words can be believed?
There are two gates to that which is believed in the Buddha’s words: first, believing in their principle; second, believing in their facts.
To believe in the principle is to believe that one's own mind is the Pure Land and that one's own nature is Amitābha. To believe in the facts is to believe in the West.

If there is truly a Pure Land in the West, then there must truly be Amitābha; though this principle exists, the principle fully constitutes the phenomenon, just as the Ocean Seal can manifest all phenomena.
Though these phenomena exist, the phenomena are entirely the principle, just as all phenomena do not depart from the Ocean Seal.
Thus, they are both one and two, yet neither one nor two. To have such faith and understanding is called... [the name of the stage].
Right faith is like believing in principle while not clinging to phenomena, or believing in phenomena while not neglecting principle; this is called biased faith, not right faith.
If a practitioner has not yet attained such right faith, they must extensively inquire from those who have prior knowledge and broadly examine the sutras and treatises;
then, all doubts will naturally melt away like ice, and right faith will naturally manifest before them, enabling them to give rise to the Great [Resolve].
One should vow to rouse great practice to attain Bodhi directly, rather than leaving it for after one's death.

There are those of exceptionally high natural aptitude who, upon merely looking at the sutras and śāstras, claim to have attained right faith; yet they are pulled down by the weight of habitual afflictions and cannot move even a single step forward.
One must know that this is merely superficial understanding and not true right faith. It is like believing that a tiger can bite a person—how could [this mere belief] suffice?
How could one dare to lightly provoke that which is like a poisonous hemlock capable of killing a man? How could one dare to taste it recklessly?

If one now willingly undergoes the calamity of being bitten by its venom yet feels no regret, what lack of faith could be more profound? If you are indeed a man of singular integrity, then please let go of this from this moment forth.

Regarding the correct practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) for those who cultivate pure karma: once one possesses right faith, one should practice the correct conduct. What is this correct conduct? It is precisely mindfulness of the Buddha.

As for the methods of mindfulness of the Buddha, many approaches are enumerated in the sutras; ancient masters have largely favored two: visualization (*guanxiang*) and recitation of the name (*chiming*). Of these two, visualization—

Regarding the single gate of holding the name: if one’s mind is coarse and understanding inferior, such that one is incapable of receiving and upholding [the teachings], then holding the name alone is the most simple, direct, and expedient method, benefiting all three faculties.
Therefore, what we now take as our primary school emphasizes exclusively the holding of the name. As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Amitābha Sūtra) says:
"If for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, or six days, one holds fast to the name..."
"Whether for one day or seven days, with single-mindedness and without confusion," and so forth, refers to this very practice of holding the name. This involves both principle and phenomenon.

As for holding by way of principle: one takes directly the four characters "A-mi-t'o-fo" as a *huatou* (critical phrase), maintaining it continuously throughout the two periods of six hours each day, neither with a mind of intentional thought, nor with a mind of non-thought, nor with a mind that is both with and without thought.

Without entertaining thoughts of existence, non-existence, or neither, one severs the continuity of past and future; with not a single thought arising, one transcends all stages to ascend directly to the stage of Buddhahood.

The practitioner who maintains this practice must focus their will and unify their contemplation, relying solely upon the single phrase "Namu Amida Butsu" as if it were Mount Sumeru—unshakable and immovable. They should recite thus in the morning and likewise in the evening.

One should likewise maintain mindfulness while walking, likewise maintain mindfulness while sitting, likewise maintain mindfulness when responding to conditions and interacting with others, and likewise maintain mindfulness even when encountering circumstances that are favorable or adverse.
With pure mindfulness continuing in succession, one will spontaneously attain the opening of the mind;

this is not in the slightest different from the previous method of upholding the principle. If one has not yet attained the opening of the mind, at the time of death, one will certainly be reborn [in the Pure Land].

That land is not for those of middling or inferior capacity. If one’s strength is insufficient or one’s practice has not yet reached purity, one must cultivate according to one’s ability—whether by performing prostrations and recitations at dawn and dusk, or by practicing the "Ten Recitations" at early morning. By accumulating merit and virtue, one gradually nurtures the fruits of goodness.

The essential point is to maintain firm faith and aspiration; then, at the moment of death, one will certainly attain rebirth there. However, because one's rank and grade are somewhat low, one will see [the following]:
The Buddha has arrived somewhat late; however, it seems he has passed the examination at the very bottom of the list, which is not necessarily a bad thing.

Furthermore, for those who cultivate various merits and pure deeds and who single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, they must extensively cultivate all manner of blessings as a prerequisite.
Zhi-zhu’s *Commentary on the Sutra of Immeasurable Life* states: "Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate the three types of merit:
first, filially supporting one's parents, serving teachers and elders, maintaining a compassionate heart and refraining from killing, and practicing the ten virtuous deeds;

second, receiving and upholding the Three Refuges, being fully endowed with the various precepts, and not violating dignified conduct; third, generating the bodhicitta, deeply believing in cause and effect, and reading [the scriptures]..."
Reciting Mahāyāna scriptures to encourage practitioners—these three types of action are the primary causes for the pure karma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.

A disciple of pure karma asked the Compassionate Illumination Guide: "If a disciple is single-mindedly practicing the *nien-fo* samādhi, may they still employ giving, upholding the precepts, making offerings, and performing meritorious deeds? The Guide replied: "If you can single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha..."
If one does not uphold the precepts, there will be the offense of transgression; if one does not practice giving, there will be the karma of long-standing stinginess and greed;
if one does not make offerings to the Triple Gem, there will be the karma of self-conceit; if one does not show respect to all, there will be the offense of despising others.

Therefore, transgressing the precepts leads to falling into hell; stinginess and greed lead to falling among the hungry ghosts; and self-conceit causes one to remain forever [in the realm of animals].
If one treats others with contempt while in the evil realms, one will be poor and lowly life after life; being thus obscured by such evil karma, how could it be possible to be born in the Pure Land?
Therefore, Master Sengzhao said: "Though the conditioned is false, if one abandons it, the Buddha-way is difficult to accomplish;

though the unconditioned is true, if one clings to it, the nature of wisdom will not be bright. You now wish to cultivate the *nien-fo* samādhi to seek rebirth—[how can you do so while harboring such thoughts?]

To swiftly attain the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi in the Pure Land, one must take the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) as the primary path, while concurrently cultivating merit and virtue as a supplementary practice.

Morning and evening, one should constantly and diligently make offerings to the Triple Gem, perform prostrations and repentance, practice giving, and maintain the precepts, thereby purifying the three karmas and further increasing pure conditions. All roots of goodness thus cultivated should be dedicated entirely toward the Pure Land.
The accomplishment of the merit of *nien-fo* through the practice of the earth [of the Pure Land] may be likened to rowing a boat with both oars and a rudder while going with the current.

Regarding the Master of Compassionate Illumination, the True Vow of *Nien-fo*, it is said: "If there is practice without the vow, that practice will surely be solitary; if there is the vow without practice, that vow will surely..."
Only when the practice of emptiness and the cultivation of vows mutually support one another can one ascend to the precious stage.

Yet, whenever I observe those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha in the present age, they may do so out of distress from illness, or to repay their parents' kindness, or to protect their homes and estates, or to prolong their lifespans.
Since such vows are not genuine, they will inevitably result in delusion; even if one practices in this way for an entire lifetime, it is all in vain.
At the moment of death, when one's life-force is spent, how could one possibly achieve rebirth [in the Pure Land] if it is not one's sincere aspiration?
Therefore, all who practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name must cultivate the right vow. This right vow is not to aspire for the blessings and rewards of humans or devas;
nor is it to aspire for the limited fruits of the provisional vehicles; nor is it to aspire for oneself alone to be born in the Pure Land and realize Bodhi. Rather, it is this:
"May all sentient beings together be born in the Pure Land and together realize Bodhi.
As soon as this vow is made, it is able to possess immeasurable merit, to eliminate immeasurable karmic defilements, and to shatter immeasurable nets of Māra;
it serves eternally as the true seed for attaining Buddhahood—this is what is called the bodhicitta. Therefore, practitioners should make such a vow every day at the appropriate time.

When the power of such a vow is thus firm and unchanging, then all myriad virtues will become the true cause for a pure land and the sublime practice of bodhi; how, then, could one worry about not being reborn there?
Although the merit of right mindfulness and pure karma is accumulated during one's ordinary days, the final thought at the moment of death is the most critical.

This is because whether one is born in the Pure Land or the defiled world, or enters the state of a sage or an ordinary person, it is solely upon this single thought that these transitions depend. Every time...
I have observed that those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha commonly speak of seeking rebirth in the Pure Land; yet, when their end approaches, many lack right mindfulness.
Some, out of a craving for life or a dread of death, cling to this physical carcass; some, looking back at their wives and children, find it difficult to endure the pain of separation;
some, being tied to family wealth, cannot let go; and some, because external conditions are unfavorable, pass away harboring resentment.
Some, oppressed by the suffering of illness, drink in the pain and depart; having already lost right mindfulness, they willingly follow the path of downfall.

Others harbor self-doubt, thinking their karma from this life is too heavy and that they have no share in the Western Land. Some doubt that they have recited the Buddha’s name for too few days and dare not hope for rebirth there.
Others harbor self-doubt, thinking their debts are not yet settled, their vows are not yet fulfilled, and their greed and anger remain unextinguished.
Regarding those who find it difficult to be reborn in that land: some harbor self-doubt, thinking, "Although I have practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, I fear the Buddha will not come to welcome me.
These four cases all involve the arising of self-generated doubts that act as obstacles, causing one to lose right mindfulness.

Furthermore, there may be those who have been diligent in mindfulness of the Buddha throughout their lives, yet suddenly fall ill and lie bedridden in deep distress, unable to endure the pain; this is due to the depth of their past karma.
What was heavy should have caused one to fall into the evil realms, but because of mindfulness of the Buddha, the heavy is transformed into light;

one should therefore endure and benefit from this by diligently practicing mindfulness of the Buddha, for one will certainly attain rebirth there. If one harbors resentment toward the Buddha-dharma, claiming it lacks efficacy, and instead gives rise to a regressive mind, one will surely fall into hell.

Or, there may be those who, though they ordinarily claim to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, harbor a deep-seated attachment to life; when illness and suffering suddenly befall them, [their resolve wavers].
They place their faith in heterodox teachers and vulgar arts, slaughtering sentient beings and burning paper money to transform it into horses as sacrifices to demonic spirits, hoping for blessings;

because their minds are thus perverted, the Buddhas do not accept their offerings. Or, due to illness, they follow the words of physicians to drink alcohol and eat meat, or even harm living beings to use as medicinal ingredients;
having already lost their roots of goodness, they will inevitably be driven by their karma. These three [categories of people...]
All have lost right mindfulness because they gave rise to obstacles due to illness. I now exhort practitioners who reach this point:
you must simply have sincere faith in the scriptural text and maintain firm, concentrated right mindfulness. Cast everything else aside and recite the Buddha’s name until the end of life.
Regard the three realms as a prison, your wife and children as enemies, your family wealth as shackles and fetters, and your own body as [a vessel of suffering].
One should conceive of the body as a stinking leather bag and as a decaying skull.
To the family members at home and to outside visitors who come to inquire after one's illness, one must first give clear instructions: they must assist by reciting the Buddha’s name;
they must not engage in idle chatter, nor discuss household affairs, nor utter sighs of lamentation, weep, or shed tears, until the body’s warmth has departed.
One may only offer lamentation once the body has been removed; if one follows this method, one will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

Even for those who have not practiced the recitation of the Buddha's name in their daily lives, there is none who cannot attain rebirth if they can follow this method. Alas! The matters of the gateway of death are of great importance;
in an instant one is born in the next life, and even a single moment’s error leads to suffering through kalpas. How can one not be careful? How can one not be careful?

Regarding the difficulty and ease of practice in the two lands, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna stated that practicing in the five turbidities is called the "difficult path," like a lame person walking on a perilous road who covers no more than a few li in a single day;
whereas practicing in the Pure Land is called the "easy path," like a weak man relying upon a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
One day, the four worlds were surveyed; now, by contrasting the ten difficulties of the Sahā world with the ten ease of the Pure Land, they are distinguished and shown.
First, in the Sahā world, one does not constantly encounter a Buddha, for Śākyamuni has already passed away and false teachings flourish;

in Sukhāvatī, however, the Buddha never ceases to exist, manifesting as the current Teacher. Second, in the Sahā world, this is an age of semblance and decadence where various non-Buddhist paths abound, even if...

In discussions of the Buddha-dharma, there are often many biases and obscurations. Regarding the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), first, the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, water-birds, and forest trees constantly proclaim the sublime Dharma.

Second, whereas in this Sahā world practitioners are enticed and deluded by evil companions who seek profit and offerings, causing them to fall into the three evil realms, in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta serve as one’s supreme friends, and all those of the highest goodness assemble together in one place.
Fourth, in the Sahā world, the various māras cause turmoil and destroy my True Dharma;

in Sukhāvatī, although there are celestial māras, they all attain the True Dharma and cause practitioners to quickly achieve accomplishment. Fifth, in the Sahā world, the cycle of rebirth in the six realms is like a water-wheel drawing from a well, with no rest;
in Sukhāvatī, one is born through transformation within a lotus flower, never again to undergo the cycle of birth and death.
Sixth, regarding the suffering of death and rebirth: in the Sahā world, beings come and go through the three realms, receiving retribution according to their karma;
even if born in the heavens, it is difficult to escape the evil paths. In Sukhāvatī, however, even the names of the three evil paths cannot be heard, let alone their actual existence.
Seventh, in the Sahā world, worldly conditions and defilements constantly act as obstacles to transcendence; in Sukhāvatī, there are only jade palaces and precious halls.
Eighth, regarding clothing, fine food, and all other requisites: in the Sahā world, people live for a hundred years, yet premature deaths are frequent;
time passes so swiftly that it is difficult to accomplish the Great Way. In Sukhāvatī, however, the lifespan of sentient beings is equal to that of the Buddha.
Ninth, regarding practice in this land: one must sever the delusions of views and thought to achieve non-retrogression; beginners in this realm cannot avoid falling back.
In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, all sentient beings who are born enter the stage of those destined for right enlightenment (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and never again regress.

Tenth, practitioners in the Sahā world find it difficult to achieve success even over kalpas as numerous as motes of dust; for instance, among those who heard the Dharma during the era of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, some who had retreated from the Great Vehicle and clung to the Small Vehicle remained as śrāvakas for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
In contrast, in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one achieves this in a single lifetime, constantly following and studying under the Buddha until the very end.
To achieve the site of enlightenment and realize supreme awakening—these ten aforementioned points of difficulty and ease differ by more than the distance between heaven and abyss.

If one relies solely on one's own strength, one will labor in vain; yet if one relies upon superior conditions, one will attain extraordinary benefits from afar. Let the practitioner choose accordingly.
Question: Since the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take great compassion as their primary vocation, they ought to dwell in evil worlds to save sentient beings from suffering.
Why, then, do they vow to be born in a Pure Land, seemingly intent only on self-benefit? Answer: Those who vow to be born in a Pure Land are not... [The text here appears to be truncated.]
It is because even for one’s own benefit, it is difficult to save suffering sentient beings if one does not take birth in the Pure Land.

As the sutras state, a bodhisattva is only permitted to mingle with the mundane world to deliver sentient beings once they have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

If this essential realization has not yet been attained, one must never be separated from a Buddha. This is because, as long as afflictions and habitual tendencies are not exhausted and the power of patience is not yet sufficient, one will inevitably encounter adverse conditions.
If one is inevitably obstructed from advancing in cultivation, it is difficult even to save oneself, let alone others.

To wish to save others while dwelling in this degenerate age is like attempting to ferry many people across the sea in a boat that is neither sound nor sturdy; it results only in both self and others drowning.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "An ordinary person bound by all fetters may possess a heart of great compassion and make such vows..."
It is impossible for one who is born into a degenerate age to save sentient beings [without relying on this path]. The *Wǎngshēng lùn* (Treatise on Rebirth) states:

"Those who wish to roam through the gates of hell shall be reborn in that land; having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they return to the cycle of birth and death to teach and transform those sentient beings suffering in hell."

Question: Those who have attained realization in the Chan school ascend directly to the stage of Buddhahood without passing through the various stages; why then do they need to aspire to be reborn in a Pure Land? Answer:
Do you mean that those who have attained realization have forever exhausted their delusions and habitual tendencies, becoming instantly identical to all Buddhas?

Or do you mean that their delusions and habitual tendencies still remain, such that they must rely on gradual cultivation? If delusions and habitual tendencies still persist, it is precisely for this reason that one should seek rebirth there.
In the Pure Land, one relies on those superior conditions to gradually refine oneself;

yet, if one wanders through the five turbidities of this world with only a meager understanding and shallow realization, remaining oblivious across lifetimes, how can one be certain of not falling back or failing?
In antiquity, masters such as Chengtian Jian, Zhenru Zhe, and Haiyin Xin were all eminent artisans of the Chan school, yet it is difficult for later generations to emulate their deeds.

If this is true for others, how much more so for one like Sudhana, a practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden path, or for Nāgārjuna, the patriarch who transmitted the Dharma-robes—both of whom were recorded as being born in Sukhāvatī? Can your realization and attainment equal those of Sudhana and Nāgārjuna?
Even if you could, it would not hinder your sharing in their birth there; yet if you have not yet attained such a level, [you must strive further].
Thus, how can the plan for rebirth be delayed? Question:

Since the mind is fundamentally free from thought and phenomena are fundamentally without arising, why does the teaching now instruct people to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and seek birth in the Pure Land?
The answer is: To take thought as thought and birth as birth is the error of eternalism;
to take non-thought as non-thought and non-birth as non-birth is the delusion of false views.
That which is thought yet without thought, and birth yet without birth, is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, within the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is no...

When one perceives even a single atom, there are no Buddhas to be mindful of and no Pure Lands to be reborn in; yet within the gateway of Buddha-activities (*buddhakārya*), not abandoning a single dharma, all the faculties are comprehensively gathered.
This is because the essential art for returning to the source lies in the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), which reveals the single gate of rebirth.
Thus, though one mindfully recites the Buddha's name all day long, it does not deviate from non-mindfulness (*amanasikāra*), and it blazes forth with intensity.
To be reborn while not deviating from non-arising— though it is said that ordinary beings and sages each abide in their own respective positions,

yet their resonance and response intersect such that, though they do not travel back and forth between east and west, the spirit transcends to the pure land; this is something that cannot be subjected to further scrutiny or contradiction.
Question: Since all Buddhas can be contemplated and all pure lands can be reborn in, why must one specifically contemplate Amitābha and seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss?
Answer: There are six reasons for this. First, because the minds of sentient beings are largely turbid and distracted, it is difficult to achieve samādhi by contemplating all Buddhas;
therefore, one must focus exclusively on a single Buddha and a single land to bind the mind to a single object, making it easy to attain [samādhi].

First, because of rebirth; second, because Amitābha’s compassionate vows are inexhaustible in receiving and guiding sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, such that even ten recitations lead to rebirth—a quality not found among other Buddhas;

third, because the adornments of merit in Sukhāvatī are of such various excellence that they differ from all other pure lands, making it easy for those who are reborn there to advance on the Path; fourth, because...
Ordinary beings lack wisdom and must rely upon the Buddha’s words;
for this Land of Ultimate Bliss is praised by Śākyamuni Buddha everywhere and by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Fifth, regarding those sentient beings who have no affinity with the Buddha and whom the Buddha cannot deliver, the sentient beings of this land—regardless of whether they are old or young, noble or humble—all know that there is [the Pure Land].

When Amitābha Buddha involuntarily lost his voice and everyone recited the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha," it was known that the sentient beings of this land share a great karmic affinity with Amitābha.

Sixth, because the essence of all Buddhas is one—wherein the one is all and the all is one—a single thought of one Buddha is the universal recitation of all Buddhas; for this reason, these six [points]...
The mind specifically points toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss; there is no greater benefit than this. Question:

To distinguish between the pure and the defiled, and to abandon the defiled while taking up the pure—all of this belongs to deluded thought (*vikalpa*). When, then, does one engage in true cultivation? Answer:
This is not the taking up and abandoning of worldly deluded thoughts; rather, it is the universal path by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transform the ordinary into the sagely.

If the Dharma were not characterized by wearying detachment (*vidūṣaṇā-prahāṇa*), how could one transform from the state of an ordinary person? If it were not characterized by joyful acceptance (*abhinandanā-parigraha*), how could one become a sage?

From the stage of an ordinary being upward, every successive level necessarily involves taking and abandoning; only upon reaching the ultimate awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) do taking and abandoning cease to exist.
Therefore, the former masters said: "The extreme of taking and abandoning is no different from the absence of taking and abandoning. This may indeed be called the non-duality of them.
Furthermore, in true cultivation, one must know that the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual and that stillness and function are without obstruction;
thus, although one engages in taking and rejecting throughout the day, one does not perceive the marks of taking and rejecting. This is what the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra means when it says:
"Though one knows that all Buddha-dharmas and sentient beings are empty, one nevertheless constantly cultivates the pure land and transforms all living beings. This is precisely what is meant.
Question: If the mind itself is the Buddha, then it should suffice to directly contemplate one's own mind; why is it necessary to recollect other Buddhas? Answer:
Since one’s own mind and all Buddhas are in reality of one and the same essence, contemplating oneself and contemplating others are both expedient means according to the capacity of the practitioner.
How could one cling to the notion that one’s own mind is the Buddha while asserting that other Buddhas exist outside of it? Furthermore, one must recollect other Buddhas.

Furthermore, this is a supreme skillful means of all Buddhas that enables one to be drawn to birth in that land by relying on the power of others, thereby swiftly reaching Bodhi; its benefit is truly great indeed.
Question: If the Pure Land is solely the mind, what is the use of seeking rebirth in Sukhāvatī? Answer:
When you say that the Pure Land is solely the mind, you are grasping at this square-inch heart as being the Pure Land, while regarding Sukhāvatī as being far away beyond ten trillion lands;
this is a complete failure to understand the principle of "solely the mind. What is meant by "solely the mind" refers to the mind...

It encompasses the great void and extends throughout the realms of sand; according to the purity of one's mind, it manifests as pure, and according to the turbidity of the mind, it manifests as turbid.
Thus we know that those born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss see purity because their own minds are pure—it is not something external to the mind.

If the mind were confined within the span of an inch, then the Pure Land would exist only there; yet if that were so, it would follow that the Land of Ultimate Bliss alone does not reside within the mind.
The Sahā world is not within the mind; it is not only that the Pure Land (Sukhāvatī) is unsuitable for birth, but the Sahā world is likewise unsuitable for birth.
Now I ask you: after this birth, will there be further birth, or will there be no further birth? If you say there is further birth, by what means will one subsequently attain "mind-only"?
If you say there is no further birth, then it is not what is being called [the state of mind-only].
"Would this not be falling into the pit of nihilism? This is the view of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and the doctrine of Pāpīyān.
Some say: "I need only purify my own mind; it will naturally accord with birth in the Pure Land. Why must one recite the Buddha's name to seek rebirth there? [The response is:
"If you do not recite the Buddha's name, you lack the conditions for the Pure Land. You merely wish to dwell in this defiled land while purifying your own mind."

This is what Nāgārjuna referred to as the "difficult path. Indeed, because the conditions and environments in this land are turbid and chaotic, they serve as many obstacles to practice—advancing seven steps and retreating eight.
One may cycle through the six realms for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, yet still remain stagnant within birth and death.

Only when the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) are exhausted can one emerge from the triple world; only upon directly realizing the seventh stage (*saptama-bhūmi*) is one termed "non-retrogressive" (*avaivartika*).
However, as long as one has not yet attained the stage of birth in the Pure Land, is it not too difficult for what is called "purity of mind" and "purity of land"?
Question: Although ordinary beings bound by all fetters recite the Buddha’s name, their greed and anger have not ceased and their minds are truly impure;
how can they be said to attain rebirth? Answer: This is due to being embraced by the power of Amitābha Buddha’s vows. The *Nāgasena Bhikṣu Sūtra* says: "It is like..."
It is like a person who, with a great boulder weighing several dozen or hundreds of *li*, wishes to cross the great ocean;
by the power of a ship, they immediately reach the other shore. The sins of sentient beings are like that great boulder, while Amitābha’s power of vows is like that great ship.

Although the stone would naturally sink, it can be crossed because of the ship; although sinners would naturally fall [into hell], they attain rebirth by relying on the Buddha. Furthermore, this applies even to those who merely "wear" [the name].
Those who attain rebirth through their karma must have possessed firm and steadfast right mindfulness at the moment their lives end;
this single thought of pure mind should immediately manifest as the Pure Land, all the more so when one has the merit of daily reciting the Buddha’s name.
Question: It is truly difficult to believe that one can attain rebirth [in the Pure Land] through ten recitations despite having committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds. Answer:

Generally speaking, the single thought at the moment of death is the most critical factor. As the sutra says, a woman who was drowning while crossing a river attained rebirth in heaven because of the wholesome thought of love for her child;
likewise, a monk who had heard nothing of the Dharma fell into hell because of the evil thought of slandering the Buddha at the moment of death.
Entering hell or attaining paradise depends on a single thought; if one can transform that thought, the Pure Land is attained through ten recitations—how could there be any doubt?
Furthermore, Amitābha Buddha made this vow: "If sentient beings call upon my name even ten times and yet are not reborn [in my land], may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Since his power of aspiration is so firm and the mind of recitation is so intense, how could one fail?
This response corresponds to that stimulus as swiftly as a shadow follows a form or an echo follows a sound;
how could there be any cause for doubt? Question: The sutra states that the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas are extinguished in every thought-moment.

This is truly a difficult-to-believe teaching; please provide a detailed explanation. Answer: These words appear in the section on the "lowest grade of rebirth" concerning the ten recitations at the moment of death. You—
One might suspect that the grave sins of birth and death accumulated over eight billion kalpas are heavy, while a single thought at the moment of death is light;
however, according to the threefold comparison of Tiantai, one cannot determine lightness or heaviness based merely on duration or quantity.
The first [comparison] concerns the mind: it refers to the mind that creates sin, which arises from one’s own false and inverted delusions, compared with the mind that recollects the Buddha.
Hearing from a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) the teaching on the true merits and the name of Amitābha Buddha gives rise to a single realization of the empty and the real;

how could these be compared? It is like a dark room ten thousand years old where the light of the sun momentarily arrives and its darkness is instantly extinguished—how could one claim that the long-standing darkness refuses to be extinguished? Second, regarding conditions: this refers to those who commit transgressions.
At that time, from a mind of false, deluded darkness, one takes false objects as conditions and gives rise to a perverted thought of mindfulness of the Buddha.
From hearing the names and titles of the Buddha’s pure and true merits, one takes supreme Bodhi as a condition and gives rise to a single mind.
How can one true and one false be compared? It is like a person struck by a poisoned arrow; the arrow is deep and the venom is cruel.
When the flesh is wounded and the bone is broken, the medicinal drum that eliminates [the poison] upon being heard causes the arrow to emerge and the venom to be removed;

how could one refuse to have it extracted simply because the arrow is deep and the venom is virulent? Third is "decisiveness," which means that at the time of committing a transgression, there is an intervening mind and a subsequent mind, whereas at the time of reciting the Buddha's name, there is no intervening mind and no subsequent mind, and thus [the transgression] is immediately eliminated.
Because the wholesome mind at the moment of death is so intense and powerful, one is reborn immediately;
it is like a rope ten spans thick that a thousand men cannot pull apart, yet a youth brandishing a sword can sever it in a mere instant.

When these three types of comparison are weighed together, they all concern the power of the mindful mind; thus, its inconceivable strength and its capacity to extinguish transgressions are already clearly evident.
However, one should understand that the name which is recited is accomplished by the myriad virtues of Amitābha Buddha and sustained by his great vows;
how could its efficacy possibly be conceived? It is like a person who takes lion sinew to make the strings of a lute:
as soon as those strings are plucked once, all other strings are simultaneously severed.
Furthermore, it is like a person who takes the milk of cattle, sheep, donkeys, and horses and places it all in a single vessel,
then drops a single drop of lion’s milk into it, causing all the other milks to be transformed entirely into water. Now, when one utters the name of the Buddha even once,
how could the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas not be extinguished?
Question: It may be granted that one can attain rebirth while still carrying karmic burdens; however, how is it possible for such a person not to fall back? Answer:
There are five causes and conditions that enable the one who has been born there not to regress: First, because they are constantly sustained by the power of Amitābha’s vows;
Second, because the Buddha’s light constantly shines upon them, causing their bodhicitta to grow ever-increasingly; Third, because the sounds of the water, birds, trees, and forests act as music.
First, all echoes proclaim suffering, emptiness, and impermanence; those who hear them constantly give rise to the mind that recollects the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

Second, that land consists purely of bodhisattvas as its virtuous friends; there are no evil environments or conditions, nor are there malevolent demons or spirits, and the afflictions of the three poisons never arise at all.
Third, their lifespan lasts for eternal kalpas, equal to that of the Buddha.
Because he is a bodhisattva.
Question: All people of the world doubt that the Land of Ultimate Bliss lies beyond ten trillion lands;

they fear that at the moment of death, in the brief span of an instant, it will be difficult to reach there. How can this be explained? Answer: Does the Sūtra not say that the mind encompasses [all things]?
If the measure of the great void encompasses the realms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, then even ten trillion lands are but within my own mind;
how could they be distant? At the moment of death, birth within my mind—how could this be difficult?

Furthermore, what are called "ten trillion lands" are spoken of only in relation to the birth-and-death mental capacity of ordinary beings with their physical eyes. If sentient beings possess the karma for a Pure Land...
For one who has attained realization, the mind in meditative concentration at the moment of death is itself the mind that takes birth in the Pure Land;

since a single movement of thought is precisely the time of being born in the Pure Land, the *Xinxinlu* states: "The fact that ten million billion lands are reached in an instant is simply because one's own mind is fundamentally wondrous."
Question: "If ten recitations at the moment of death can indeed lead to rebirth in the Pure Land, we shall simply attend to our other karmic tasks and wait for those final ten recitations.
How is this? Answer: "Rebirth through ten recitations occurs but once in ten thousand cases; do you wish to rely on such a remote chance?
Generally, those who achieve the ten recitations at the moment of death do so because their past roots of goodness are powerful, which induces such a result."
To encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) at the time of death and achieve the ten recitations is rare;

if one lacks the karma that brings about such a spiritual friend, it is difficult even to meet one, let alone achieve the ten recitations. Furthermore, the *Qunyi lun* enumerates ten types of people who cannot practice Buddha-recitation at the end of life:
first, those who do not necessarily encounter virtuous friends and have no one to exhort them to recite the Buddha’s name. Second...
1. Karma and suffering entangle the body, leaving no leisure to recite the Buddha’s name; 2. Or one suffers from a stroke that causes loss of speech, making it impossible to invoke the Buddha;
3. Or one is deranged and loses the mind, making focused contemplation difficult to achieve; 4. Or one encounters water or fire, leaving no time for sincere devotion; 5.
Or one meets with jackals and wolves, finding no virtuous friends to assist; 6. Or at the moment of death, evil associates corrupt the dying person.

The eight types of those who die through lack of faith are: first, death by drowning; second, death by fire; third, death by being struck by lightning; fourth, death by falling into a pit; fifth, death by being crushed under a collapsing building; sixth, death from eating food that causes illness;

seventh, death from excessive consumption of food and drink leading to stupor; eighth, sudden death on the battlefield during combat; ninth, sudden death from falling from a high cliff and injuring one's life;

and tenth, sudden death from other such evil conditions. If one suddenly encounters even one of these ten types of calamities, one’s life comes to an end. Can one still recite the Buddha’s name? Even if you were free from these ten kinds of misfortunes—
When encountering adverse conditions, even dying of a terminal illness cannot avoid the "wind-sword" that dismembers the body and the separation of the four elements;
like a living turtle shedding its shell, one is oppressed by such agony—can you still recite the Buddha’s name?

Or when worldly affairs are not yet concluded and worldly thoughts have not ceased, with a mind agitated by the fear of death and the craving for life—can you still recite the Buddha’s name? Or when a father...
The mother sheds tears and the wife and children weep in sorrow; their lingering attachment is unbearable, and their grief wounds the heart.
Should one not then call upon the Buddha? How can you fail to consider this, waiting until the final moments for ten recitations, only to bring about your own ruin?
Question: Reciting the Buddha’s name is considered a practice for after death; I do not know whether it also brings benefit in the present life. Answer:
The sutras explain in detail that those who receive and uphold the Buddha’s name shall obtain ten kinds of benefits:

first, day and night they will constantly be protected by all the great powerful devas and divine generals, with retinues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who remain invisible to guard them. Second, they will constantly...
First, twenty-five great bodhisattvas, such as Avalokiteśvara and others, as well as all bodhisattvas, will constantly follow and protect them;
second, they will always receive the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas day and night, and Amitābha Buddha will constantly emit light to gather in and sustain this person;
third, no malevolent spirits whatsoever will be able to harm them, nor any venomous snakes.

Fifth, neither venomous dragons nor poisonous drugs can take effect; one shall not suffer from the calamities of fire or water, nor from enemies, thieves, swords, arrows, imprisonment, shackles, or drills, nor from untimely death or madness.
Sixth, all previously committed karmic actions shall be completely extinguished;
those whose lives were taken by them shall attain liberation, and no further retribution or opposition shall arise. Seventh, in dreams at night, one shall see [only] what is correct...
Eighth, one may directly or in dreams behold the sublime and wondrous form of Amitābha Buddha;
ninth, the mind is constantly joyful, the complexion is radiant and bright, physical strength is abundant, and all actions are auspicious;
tenth, one is always honored, supported, and joyfully prostrated to by all people of the world, as if venerating a Buddha; eleventh, at the end of life...

At that time, the mind is free from fear and right mindfulness manifests; one beholds Amitābha Buddha and the assembly of holy beings, who receive one with golden lotus flowers and lead one to rebirth in the Western Pure Land, where one shall enjoy supreme and wondrous bliss until the end of the future.

As for the ten kinds [of benefits] mentioned above, both those pertaining to the present life and those pertaining to future rebirths possess superior harmony. Thus, regarding both worldly and world-transcending matters...
It is indeed true that among the essential and urgent Dharma-gates, none is equal to the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation).

Question: Since the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang Shijie*) is the transformation realm of our Original Teacher [Vairocana], why do we not seek birth in the Flower Treasury World, but instead seek birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Jile*)?
Answer: This very question appears within the *Huayan Shu* (Commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra). Therein, four reasons are given for this: first, ... [the rest of the text follows].
First, because there is a specific condition: namely, that Amitābha’s vows are profound and specifically embrace the people of this Sahā world.
Second, because it causes sentient beings to take refuge with a single-minded devotion: within the Flower Treasury World (Huazang), worlds are infinite;

if one hears that all ten directions are wondrous, beginners will be bewildered and have no place to rely upon, so he uses skillful means to lead them by pointing exclusively to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Third, [it is for the sake of... (the text continues).

Because it is not separate from the Flower Treasury (Kusumatalagarbha), although the Land of Ultimate Bliss is said to be ten trillion lands away from here, since all Flower Treasury Buddha-lands are as numerous as motes of dust, one knows that they are not separate. Fourth, because it is the very Teacher himself: the entire ocean of Flower Treasury lands is the realm of Vairocana;
since these ten trillion lands have not yet transcended the midst of a single land-cluster (kṣetradhātu), is this not the Teacher manifesting according to names?
This is a transformation.
A questioner asks: "The sutras state that those born in Tuṣita will descend with Maitreya Bodhisattva to be among the three assemblies and naturally attain the fruits of the Path.
Why then must one abandon Tuṣita nearby and seek Sukhāvatī from afar? The answer is: You...
To say that Tuṣita is near and Sukhāvatī is far is merely spoken from the perspective of the mental capacity of ordinary beings with their physical eyes.
Since all three realms reside within a single mind, and the mind itself makes no distinction between "self" and "other," how can it be said that Tuṣita is near and Sukhāvatī is far?
Furthermore, when comparing and weighing Tuṣita and Sukhāvatī against one another, there are ten points of difference.

First, regarding the difference in superiority and inferiority: it is possible to be reborn in Sukhāvatī through ten recitations, whereas rebirth in Tuṣita requires the cultivation of various samādhis and deep entry into right concentration; thus, rebirth in the latter is more difficult.

Second, Sukhāvatī possesses the power of Amitābha Buddha’s great compassionate vows, which pledge to extend his grace and receive beings; in Tuṣita, however, Maitreya has no such vow of reception. Third...

First, as for the extreme bliss [of Sukhāvatī], it is because the great power of Amitābha Buddha’s radiance touches the bodies and minds of practitioners, bringing them harmony and compassion so that they are reborn in that land—a state not found even in Tuṣita. Fourth, Amitābha Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is ten times greater than that of all other Buddhas;
furthermore, sentient beings naturally hear whatever teachings they wish to hear according to their own inclinations and desires. This is also not found in Tuṣita.

First, regarding that which Tuṣita lacks and Sukhāvatī possesses: in the Land of Ultimate Bliss there are no women to disturb sentient beings, whereas in Tuṣita the celestial maidens are so exquisite that the gods become infatuated with them and are unable to exert themselves toward spiritual progress. Second, regarding that which Tuṣita lacks and Sukhāvatī possesses:

those born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss all attain the thirty-two primary marks and eighty secondary signs, and are fully endowed with supernormal powers; these are absent in Tuṣita. Third, regarding that which Sukhāvatī... [text truncated]
Those who take birth in Tuṣita naturally subdue and extinguish their afflictions and immediately ascend to the stage of non-retrogression;
although they daily preach the Dharma of non-retrogression to transform sentient beings, it is not necessarily the case that they have already ascended to non-retrogression.
Eighth, those who take birth in Sukhāvatī go directly from this single lifetime to the site of enlightenment to achieve unsurpassed awakening, whereas in Tuṣita, one descends with the Buddha.
Those born there do not necessarily realize the fruits of sainthood, let alone the unsurpassed enlightenment.
Ninth, those born in Sukhāvatī attain immeasurable life, equaling that of the Buddha—a state not found even in Tuṣita.

Tenth, those born in Sukhāvatī who wish to make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions will find that the requisite offerings appear spontaneously before them at their mere wish, in an instant.
Pervading the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas, one returns to one's own land of Tuṣita at the very time of eating.

These ten aforementioned points of comparison regarding superiority and inferiority are evident; yet, if one seeks them with subtlety, there should be immeasurable practitioners—each should choose for themselves.
Question: Some claim that the Pure Land is merely a skillful means (*upāya*) of the sages to guide those of dull faculties and transform the vessels of ordinary beings.
If one could transcend directly and enter the stage of the Tathāgata all at once, what need would there be for the power of another? Answer:

In the past, Mañjuśrī attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) because he practiced mindfulness of the Buddha; Sudhana sought birth [in the Pure Land] by means of the ten great kings of vows.

If even Śāntarakṣita and Avalokiteśvara entered samādhi by recollecting the Buddha and mindfulness of the Buddha, and if King Śuddhodana along with sixty thousand members of the Śākya clan were all reborn in that Pure Land—can these truly be called those of dull faculties or ordinary vessels? Furthermore, the Buddha told Maitreya:
"In this world, there are sixty-seven billion non-retrogressive bodhisattvas who will be reborn in that land."
Each and every bodhisattva has already made offerings to countless Buddhas, being equal in merit to Maitreya.
The number of bodhisattvas of minor practice and those who have cultivated few roots of virtue is beyond calculation;
they shall all be reborn there—not only in my land, but also in other Buddha-fields, such as the realm of the Buddha Dūraprabhāsa, where there are eighteen billion [Buddha-lands].
All Bodhisattvas shall be reborn in the immeasurable Buddha-fields of the ten directions; those who are reborn are incalculable.
Even if I were to explain this in detail for an entire eon, I could not exhaust it; would it be right to call such a person of dull faculties and ordinary capacity one who has reached the end?
As for the claim that the Pure Land is merely a skillful means of the sages, this is actually a provisional teaching within the definitive doctrine.
Skillful means (*upāya*) is not a provisional teaching; the distinction between the provisional and the real within the various schools of doctrine does not follow a single path.
The judgments of both the Tiantai and Xianshou schools alike do not fail to recommend the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Avataṃsaka* as the most authentic.
Now, observing the "Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it states that if a woman hears this sutra and practices according to its teachings, her life—

At the end of life, one will be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), attain the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of a bodhisattva, and realize the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* has not yet been encountered, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra instructs Sudhana to cultivate the ten great kings of vows;

at the end of life, he will be guided to rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and shall before long attain enlightenment. Thus, it is known that the merit of recollecting the Buddha is equal to hearing [the teachings].
The merit of practicing according to the teachings of the Lotus Sutra is exactly equal to the merit of generating the ten great kings of vows;
since both sutras are judged to be definitive (nītārtha), it can be known that the Pure Land [teachings] are not provisional (neyārtha).
Furthermore, even if they are called provisional, it can be understood that they are the skillful means of the definitive teaching. Moreover, I have previously examined this matter.

The *Awakening of Faith* states: "When a beginner first cultivates right faith in the Mahāyāna, they may fear that because they do not constantly encounter the Buddha in this land, their faith will lack the necessary conditions and thus degenerate.
One should know that the Tathāgata possesses a supreme skillful means to ensure they do not regress;
one need only single-mindedly contemplate Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, whose true nature is the Dharmakāya, and one will certainly be born there."
That country has also examined the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*. The Sūtra says: "Ordinary beings have weak and inferior mental conceptions;
they have not yet attained the divine eye and cannot see from afar. The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess extraordinary skillful means (*upāya*) to enable them to see.

Now, what is called a "superior skillful means" or an "extraordinary skillful means"—is this not expedient means (*upāya*)? Since these two are discussed in terms of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), then this...

This provisional [teaching] is thus non-dual and indistinguishable from the subtle and wondrous skillful means of the *Lotus Sūtra*; therefore, it is called the "skillful provisional means of the True Teaching.
Question: Practitioners of Chan meditation often say that Chan is the real [teaching] while Buddha-recitation is provisional, and that Chan is sudden while [Buddha-recitation is gradual].
"Is the Buddha gradual or not? He replied, "You see the recitation of a single phrase of the Buddha’s name and call it provisional;
you see the holding of a single phrase of the *huatou* and call it real. You do not realize that if the Buddha’s name can be called provisional, then the *huatou* likewise cannot be called real.
Have you not seen that the secret scriptures of the Tripiṭaka and the bequeathed words of the Five Lamps are all..."
This stinking, rotting, entangling wisteria kills people; it is like an empty fist or yellow leaves used to deceive a child into stopping its crying.

Thus we know that when the Buddhas of the three periods and the patriarchs of successive generations opened their two flaps of skin to speak for the sake of others, there was nothing that was not expedient means (*upāya*).

Even that which one has personally entered is likewise nothing but expedient means. Although it is said to be "straightforwardly abandoning expedient means and speaking directly," there is no such thing as direct speech without expedient means.
The Supreme Way is already expedient from the very beginning. For example, in the Lotus Sūtra, the first cycle of teaching is called the "Expedient Means" chapter;
is this not provisional? Thus we know that both the recitation of the Buddha's name and the practice of Zen meditation are established as skillful means to guide and lead beings toward realization.
Once realized, they are nothing but the Real; before realization, they are nothing but the provisional. As for what you say—
Those who claim that Chan is a sudden teaching argue that the mere non-arising of a single thought is itself called Buddhahood. Consider this:

when one recollects the Buddha and contemplates the Buddha until the mind opens and one beholds the Buddha, is there any difference in depth between that state and the non-arising of a single thought?

Furthermore, the gradual teachings of the Mahāyāna frequently speak of traversing three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and cultivating the practices of the six *pāramitās*, yet even so, one still requires a hundred kalpas [to reach the final stage].
Only after planting the causes for the various marks and signs does one subsequently attain perfect enlightenment;
those born in this Pure Land immediately ascend to the stage of non-retrogression, becoming fully endowed with the thirty-two major marks, the eighty minor signs, and immeasurable supernormal powers.

Their lifespan is immeasurable, and they attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime—how could this be within the reach of the gradual teachings? Furthermore, even the water birds and the forest trees [all proclaim the Dharma].
The jeweled nets that emit wondrous sounds and the celestial music all proclaim the sublime Dharma; thus, it belongs neither exclusively to the gradual nor is it restricted to the sudden.
To now categorize this as the fruit of the gradual—on what basis is such a claim made?
It is nothing more than the baseless chatter of the mad and blind, leading one another into confusion and delusion.
