Regarding the precept against taking life, the Buddhist tradition regards it as the most fundamental; this is not merely a private assertion of Buddhism.

It is because, according to the nature of all beings—both human and non-human—that which is most cherished is life, and that which is most dreaded is death; therefore, they loathe [the act of killing].
Among the most grievous of all sins, none is weightier than killing. Furthermore, we have heard that the greatest virtue of Heaven and Earth is called "life";
from this, we know that the greatest evil of humanity is called "taking life. Since the Supreme Lord (Shangdi) loves life, we know that what He detests is the taking of life.
Since benevolence is the foremost of all goodness, we know that the taking of life is the foremost of all evils. Thus, the man of perfect virtue—
If it is the mind, then one knows that killing living beings is not the human heart; should the precept against killing not be regarded as weighty?

Furthermore, since humans take benevolence (*ren*) as their mind, its capacity encompasses empty space—how could there be any place where it is paralyzed or withered? Its mechanism penetrates from beginning to end—how could there be any time when it ceases or extinguishes?
That which is called "heaven, earth, and the myriad things as one body" is precisely this mind; it is precisely this benevolence.

Therefore, when the sages of the Confucian school attain the harmony of the Mean (*zhonghe*), they must reach the ultimate point where heaven and earth are established in their proper places and all things are nurtured;

when they cultivate perfect sincerity (*zhencheng*) to exhaust their own nature, they must reach the ultimate point where they can exhaust the nature of all things. This is neither far-fetched nor extravagant;

it is simply how the benevolence of the single body (*yiti zhi ren*) fundamentally is. Since the benevolence of the single body is fundamentally thus, it is nonetheless unavoidable that the sage’s governance of the world...
As for the consumption of fresh food, it was because the sages had no choice. I have examined the Buddhist scriptures:
at the beginning of the kalpa, the people were simple and sincere, so Heaven produced earth-fertility and non-glutinous rice to provide for their daily needs.
Later, as the calculating mind gradually grew, both the earth-fertility and the non-glutinous rice ceased to grow, and the people...

Scarcity of food led to being oppressed by the fires of hunger; the impulse for killing was perversely stirred, such that the strong bullied the weak and the wise bullied the foolish, seizing birds and beasts to eat them—no different from birds and beasts devouring one another.

Thus, while the initial plan was to block their hunger, they eventually came to crave the stench of raw flesh; day by day this grew worse, and slaughter ran rampant. It was at this point that the Sage arose.
Out of compassion for them, he established the rites to provide protection for them, decreeing: "In the second month of spring, one must not permit the destruction of nests or the breaking of eggs;

fish less than one chi in length shall not be sold; sacrifices must be conducted according to the rites with regular provisions; banquets must be conducted according to the rites with a fixed number of guests;
Great Officers shall not slaughter oxen or sheep except for a grave reason; and scholars shall not slaughter dogs or pigs except for a grave reason."
Could this possibly be the fundamental intention of the Sage? Unable to stop what beings naturally incline toward, he merely provided a means to prevent their excessive transgression;
thus it is said that this was the Sage’s unavoidable necessity. For although things and myself are separated by physical forms, our consciousnesses are in fact identical.
In our craving for life and dread of death, how are we any different from others? Yet now, one inflicts upon them infinite and ultimate suffering.
To sustain myself for a mere moment of trivial pleasure—is this peaceful in sentiment? Is it appropriate in principle?

To take that most precious life and limb to enjoy my own idle and superficial human sentiments—is this peaceful in sentiment? Is it appropriate in principle? To kill another’s life in the hope of prolonging my own life;
to kill another’s body in the hope of nourishing my own body; to kill another’s parents, wife, and children... [is this peaceful in sentiment? Is it appropriate in principle?]
If you, as a son, hope to preserve your own parents, wife, and children—is this peaceful in terms of human feeling? Is it appropriate in terms of principle?
Even without waiting for self-reflection, consider by extension the state of those being slaughtered upon the blade and the block, or cast alive into boiling cauldrons;
can their expressions of terror and wailing, their agony and resentment, truly be endured? Can they truly be eaten? If you think they can be endured—
When eating, one’s mind is already no longer that of a human being. Mencius said: "A gentleman, seeing its life, cannot bear to see its death;
hearing its cry, he cannot bear to eat its flesh. How could this be a matter of mere private sentiment or indulgence?

As for the world in recent times, there is even more that is不忍言 (unbearable to speak of); social customs have become shallow and corrupt, people compete in the pursuit of frivolity and luxury, exhausting themselves in the pursuit of fine flavors.
In their desire for delicacies, they exhaust every rarity found on land and in water; for a single meal, they slaughter hundreds of living beings.
Most grievous of all is that during the mourning period for parents, they drink wine and eat meat as if at a celebratory banquet, killing countless creatures.
This alone is a grave violation of the rites of the ancient sages and a transgression against [the laws] of recent times.
To harbor resentment and seek vengeance against one's enemies abroad, while internally destroying the bonds of benevolence and filial piety—is this to be called Confucianism? Is it not?
Is this to be called goodness? Is it not? Whenever someone attempts to admonish them, they invariably use worldly censure and suspicion as an excuse.
Such people neither fear the sacred statutes, nor the royal laws, nor the reality of their own unrighteousness and lack of filial piety.
I alone fear the frivolous criticisms of the secular world—what is their basis? What indeed is their basis? Alas!
While it is natural for ordinary and ignorant folk to follow the customs of the age, how could a man of heroic character acquiesce to them without scrutiny? Long ago, Huang Shan-gu composed a verse:
"My flesh and the flesh of sentient beings differ in form, yet their substance is not different; fundamentally, we share the same single nature."
It is merely that one must endure physical suffering for others while reserving rich and savory foods for oneself;
do not allow the Lord of Yama to pass judgment upon you. Reflect upon this for yourself: how does this accord with the intent of the precept against killing? This verse exhausts the matter.

As for the doctrine of cause and effect and karmic retribution, it is logically inevitable and impossible to evade; it is not only detailed in the Buddhist scriptures, but is also recorded in secular historical chronicles.

What is witnessed and heard by the ears and eyes is clear and beyond doubt; yet the gentleman’s cessation of evil is not for fear of punishment, nor is his practice of benevolence for the sake of seeking reward—it is simply to preserve his own humanity. May those of lofty intelligence take note of this.

Regarding the drowning of a woman in the ocean of karma, I have heard that among all karmic actions, the killing of a living being is the most grave; among acts of killing, the killing of a human being is the most grave;
among the killing of humans, the killing of one’s own father or son is the most grave; and among the killing of sons, [it is the killing of one who is... without...
Among all sins, killing is the most grave. That the common world today practices female infanticide is precisely what is called killing innocent children—a transgression of the greatest magnitude.
Yet the world remains complacent and takes no offense at this, regarding it as a mere constant; is this not truly extraordinary?
Formerly, Mencius said that when people today suddenly see a child about to fall into a well, they all experience a sense of alarm and compassionate pity.
The mind does not act to win favor from the parents of the child, nor to seek praise from the village and its friends, nor because it loathes the child's reputation;
it simply says that one who lacks a heart of compassion is not human.
Now, to lift up your own child and drown him is to love your child less than the neighbor's child. It is not only this; even within the prison...
When a prisoner’s crime is such that he ought to be executed, the judicial officials still defer the sentence until autumn or winter to prolong his life for even a brief moment;
yet now you lift up a woman and drown her—this is to love a child more than a prisoner facing death for his crimes. Not only this:
the compassionate and sympathetic feelings of a benevolent person pervade all things; even toward wriggling insects and crawling creatures, one cannot bear to harm them. Now...
To take up one's daughter and drown her shows that one’s love for a child does not extend even to the most minute of crawling insects. This is not all;

among those who are most cruel and obstinate, none surpass birds and beasts. Yet, we hear that a monkey’s bowels were torn asunder out of grief for its offspring, and a tiger looked back repeatedly to gaze upon its young.
How could such affection for a child ever distinguish between male and female? Now, to take up one’s daughter and...
To drown one’s own child is a lack of benevolence even compared to that of birds and beasts.

For those who act as parents yet behave in such a manner, let us set aside for a moment the fact that they will face the retribution of execution in this life and the severance of their lineage in the afterlife;

consider instead how, the moment they leave the mother’s womb, they are cast away at the place of death—unable to cry out, with suffering beyond remedy, they wallow and twist in mountain streams and ravines.
Among those on the road, even passersby dare not look directly at him; as for those who are his parents, can they truly bear to do so, or cannot?
Alas! That which distinguishes humans from birds and beasts is their possession of a heart that cannot bear [to harm others].
Now, his heart has become so callous that he is not even equal to a bird or beast; how can he claim to have received the mandate of Heaven?
Between the earth and heaven, I have often sought deeply into the cause of this matter, yet I am unable to resolve it myself.

Is it that you, having served another family, feel no concern for the succession of the lineage and thus drown [the child]? But do you not say that when a son is born, he may wander in all directions—what can be done about that?
Is it that you wish to save on the expenses of the dowry and therefore drown him? But do you not also say that when a son is born...?
If one gambles away wealth or squanders it on prostitution until the family estate is ruined, what can be done? Is this because you anticipated his lack of virtue and thus indulged him?
Yet have you not said that if a son is born, he will bring disgrace upon the family’s reputation—what then can be done? Is it because the family is poor and difficult to sustain that you indulge him?
Yet have you not said that if a son is born, he must be clothed and fed—what then can be done? Is it because there is nothing... [to provide for him]?

Is it because there are more men than women that they drown them? Yet you alone do not say: "Having received this karmic retribution from the unseen world, and having no sons for the rest of one's life, what can be done?
To examine the origin of this practice, it is nothing more than taking killing as a constant habit until the heart of benevolence has utterly perished.

They conform to the ways of the vulgar, deceive themselves by claiming the royal law takes no notice, and pursue only the interests of their private households, showing no fear of the punishment of ghosts and spirits.
When one uses their ears to hear of such a woman, her feelings of grievance and resentment would surely pierce the sun and cause frost to fall;
as for her parents, their discordant and inauspicious vapors must surely shroud the heavens and obscure the universe.

Is this not the commission of a most heinous offense and the bequeathing of endless calamity? It causes my eyes to meet with distress and my heart to be wounded; it is for this reason that I speak thus.
I urge you with eloquence to pray for the power to change this situation and to persuade [the other party] to turn the wind [of fate].
If you should encounter someone who would abandon their daughter, you might act as an intermediary to preserve her life; this may well be an opportunity to transform misfortune into good fortune.
Exhortation to Release Living Beings:
I have often heard that the Buddhas and sentient beings are of one mind. The Buddhas cultivate their Great Compassion through the love of sentient beings;
therefore, their compassion is supreme. Sentient beings take the compassion of the Buddhas and seal it as their own love; therefore, their love is profound.
There is no love deeper than the deepest love, yet none is more loving than protecting one's own life;
there is no compassion greater than the greatest compassion, yet none is more compassionate than saving the lives of others.

Therefore, that the gentlemen of antiquity delighted in the release of living beings was truly because they embodied the great compassion of all Buddhas above and fulfilled the profound love of sentient beings below.
What could be greater than this for the goodness of a virtuous person? Alas, once the mechanism of death is triggered, cruel and poisonous deeds are widely practiced.
By a hundred schemes they are hunted down, and by a thousand stratagems they are seized. Some are tightly confined within cages and enclosures; others are hung alive upon knives and carving blocks.

Their courage fails and their souls flee; mothers are separated from their children. With mouths full of indignation, to whom can they cry out? With eyes wide and staring, they seek aid in vain. This is truly... [the situation].
It is like a prisoner awaiting execution who has drawn near the gate of death, or like a community in retreat that is suddenly seized by bandits;
what can be said of the state of their acute suffering and their piteous resentment?

For this reason, the Buddhas have strictly prohibited killing in the face of such suffering and have extensively exhorted the release of living beings, urging one to sacrifice one's own insubstantial wealth to redeem the most precious lives of others, even if it be but a small amount.
Whether it be one, two, or more, up to ten thousand, he causes those who were in peril to find safety and those on the brink of death to return to life.
Though the heavens are high and the seas are vast, they may roam at will; though the sun is warm and the breeze is gentle, they shall all return to the Great Peace (*xihao*).
Although this may be called the smallest of acts, it is in truth a virtue of the greatest magnitude—let alone considering whether these beings will become future Buddhas or many others.
One's biological parents, knowing that they share the same nature as all beings, must find this difficult to endure;

it matters not whether they receive retribution before their death or compensation after their passing, for once the vital spark of life is touched, the emotion naturally becomes impossible to forget.
Moreover, when seeing the yellowing and falling of grasses and trees, one feels sorrowful; and beholding the gloom and severity of clouds and mist, one still feels a profound melancholy.
The loss of happiness serves as proof that the true mind must pervade the ten voids; the Great Benevolence flows directly through the myriad species.
How could those possessing blood and breath lack the sincerity of compassionate pity?

I only pray that you will constantly practice salvation so that the pulse of benevolence may flow eternally, widely exhorting your peers so that the wind of compassion may be universally spread, thereby perfecting one's original nature.
By preserving oneself, one honors the imperial benevolence that all Buddhas extol;
thus, the momentum of the cycle of slaughter is silently turned back. This is what is called "the greatest joy of doing good," and it is surely a magnificent feat of the Great Peace.
I pray you will extend a single hand rather than knitting your brows in frown.

Regarding the inquiry on the origin of things within the precept against killing: "Things originally were not things; their arising is likewise without arising. One need only realize that the mind itself is the subtle completion of the myriad things. [The questioner asks: "Is it not the case that even throwing oneself off a cliff or cutting off one's own flesh still belongs to the realm of conditioned action (*saṃskṛta*), and that ransoming oysters and releasing snails merely results in increased toil and expense? The answer says: The sages of antiquity established the prohibitions against killing because they feared that the hearts of the people would become callous. Thus, they enacted laws to prohibit the taking of life, yet they did not forbid the compassionate rescue of those already caught. This is because the intention to save life is superior to the act of killing; the former is a manifestation of the Way, while the latter is a transgression of the law. If one can truly understand that the mind is the source of all phenomena, then even the practice of self-sacrifice is not ultimately different from the act of saving life. However, if one does not understand this principle, then such acts of self-sacrifice are merely the cultivation of merit through conditioned effort. To claim that ransoming oysters and releasing snails is merely a waste of labor and resources is a narrow view that fails to grasp the profound intent of the sages. If one’s heart is set upon the Great Way, then every act of compassion contributes to the transformation of beings. If one’s heart is set upon worldly gain, then even great sacrifices will yield no spiritual fruit. It is said: "The Way is not far; it lies right before one. How could the Way be limited by the boundaries of conditioned phenomena? It is simply a matter of whether or not one’s own mind is capable of responding to it. Therefore, do not disparage the practice of saving life; rather, strive to cultivate the mind that gives rise to such acts. Only then will you truly be practicing the Way.
When one exhaustively investigates the ultimate principle, what death is there and what life? Yet, when conforming to the sentiments of sentient beings, one rejoices in life and grieves for death.
This is because the multitude of existences is the realm of true non-existence, and engagement with phenomena is the gateway to the integration of principle.
If one clings to non-action while being ill at ease with active existence, then talk of non-action merely serves to fuel stinginess; if one clings to non-arising...

To criticize the practice of releasing living beings is to undermine the teaching of non-arising and, in turn, assist greed and cruelty. Since one can eat meat without hindrance to true cultivation, how could releasing living beings be contrary to the sublime principle?
This is what is meant by saying that when one throws oneself off a cliff or cuts off one's own flesh, the attachment to the body is utterly forgotten;
when one feeds a starving tiger or a hawk, the compassionate heart becomes ever more expansive. By exercising this compassionate heart, the merit of conditioned action becomes manifest.

To eliminate attachment to the body is to accord in mystery with the principle of non-arising; yet now, that which you value is your own person, while that which you disregard is the life of other beings.
Since you cherish your own life so intensely as to cling to it, to take the lives of others under the pretext of being free from birth and death is nothing short of the height of inhumanity.
Question: The sutras state that "that which is neither born nor extinguished does not arise, and thus does not perish;
whereas that which has birth has extinction. If this is so, what obstacle is there to taking life? Answer: The sutras state that the mark of all dharmas is emptiness;

they are fundamentally unborn and likewise unextinguished. Because they are unborn, they are eternally quiescent; because they are unextinguished, they are eternally luminous. This eternal quiescence and eternal luminosity is called the "Eternal" (Nitya).
The Land of Tranquil Light corresponds here to the wondrous mind of man; how can such discourse on the ultimate truth be turned into frivolous sophistry?
That the deluded explanations of fools have reached this point is truly lamentable.
Question: Since it is difficult for sentient beings to escape their fixed karma (*niyata-karma*), what is the use of releasing them? Answer:

All who possess life share the same nature, and all who fear death share the same sentiment. If one argues that because the lives of animals are difficult to preserve they ought to be slaughtered for cooking, does this mean that human life, being brief, may likewise be taken at will?
Furthermore, those prisoners destined for execution in the dungeons must inevitably pass through the various stages of the penal system.
In autumn and winter, when treating those on their deathbeds with life-threatening illnesses, physicians still wish to prolong their stay for days and nights;
yet this involves a certainty of death while still hoping for life—how much more so the case of one who is actually alive and not necessarily destined to die immediately?
The questioner asked, "Virtuous One, you ought to broadly save the masses of living beings; why attend to such minor acts of compassion toward insignificant creatures?
He replied, "Matters may be grand or minute, but the mind knows no distinction between great and small. Whether grasping an elephant or seizing a rabbit, the lion’s full strength is present in both.

Whether it be a slender blade of grass or a towering forest, the universal drenching of a single rain makes no difference. It is not that the mind is not great; how could it disdain doing good because the deed is small?"
It is not that [the good] is small; how could one see that small goodness is not great?

If it were necessarily as you say, then the construction of ponds and reservoirs would lack the merit of Duke Xiang of Zheng, and the "praying net" would surely not have been the strategy of King Yin. It is simply that we value the expansion and fulfillment of the good.

Question: Since releasing living beings is certainly an act of compassion, why is it that one does not release chickens, pigs, geese, and ducks, but instead releases only fish, birds, eels, and loaches?
Is this not a form of inequality? Answer: There are two kinds of animals in the world.
The first are those who experience the fixed fruit of being killed, such as chickens, pigs, and the like. The second are those who experience the unfixed fruit of being killed, such as fish.
Birds and the like are such [beings]; the fruit of intentional killing cannot be averted, whereas the fruit of unintentional killing can be averted.
This distinction arises from the differences in the karma created by sentient beings; it is not that the mind of compassion is unequal.
Question: When entertaining guests and hosting banquets, if one does not kill living beings, it would greatly contradict human sentiment and inevitably lead to criticism and suspicion;

what should be done? Answer: When Confucius followed the common folk from below, did he consider it a matter of reproach to go against the masses? When Mencius was fond of debate, did he feel shame because of people’s criticisms?
It is simply that we maintain our own principles; how could this hinder others from expressing their disapproval? This is all the more so in the case of the True Dharma of the Buddhas.
Wisdom perceives the great benefit and harm of ten thousand kalpas, whereas the deluded sentiments of worldly people perceive only the minor gains and losses of a single moment.
If one follows the deluded sentiments of sentient beings, one may avoid censure for a time, yet will inevitably undergo the great suffering of ten thousand kalpas;
if one follows the correct wisdom of the Buddhas, though one may not avoid [censure] for a single...
If one avoids the censure of the world at this time, one will surely obtain eternal bliss for ten thousand kalpas. The Buddha’s teaching must not be transgressed;
what need is there to worry about the words of men? It is for the wise to choose accordingly. Question:
Fish, shrimp, eels, and loach—these lives are most minute, yet those killed in a single day are beyond counting. If one kills these...
If one commits a transgression, all people shall fall together into the three miserable realms. The answer is: there are those who kill such beings yet do not fall into the three realms;
this is because the power of other wholesome deeds is strong, and thus they may temporarily escape. However, once the retribution for those wholesome deeds is exhausted, their downfall is inevitable.
Furthermore, although the categories of sentient beings are minute, all possess Buddha-nature; to kill even a single minute life is likewise to kill one [Buddha].
O Son of the Buddha, people often disregard the subtle details and commit vast slaughter; they take the lives of thousands before even satisfying the need for a single meal.
Causing them to die in agony while one indulges in the taste of a mere moment’s saliva—how can such food be eaten when the grievance of ten thousand kalpas remains unresolved?
Question: Is observing the fast and abstaining from meat superior to releasing living beings? Answer:

The reason the Buddha taught people to observe the fast is precisely because he wished for them to broaden their minds of compassion. Compassion (*maitrī*) means bestowing joy, while pity (*karuṇā*) means extracting [beings] from suffering.
Now, if one observes the fast but does not release living beings, what can be called "bestowing joy," and what can be called "extracting from suffering"?

Even though one does not eat meat, it is still called a "great violation of the fast. Furthermore, the Buddha has three sets of pure precepts (*tri-śīla-skandha*): first, the precept of restraining misconduct (*saṃvara-śīla*);
second, the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*); and third, the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).

Now, not eating meat is the precept of restraining misconduct; releasing living beings is the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas; and teaching others to refrain from killing is the precept of benefiting sentient beings.

Releasing living beings is the precept of benefiting sentient beings. To now refuse to release them and even to teach others that they need not do so is likewise called a great violation of the precepts. Alas!

If even our Buddha cut flesh from his own body to ransom a dove, how can those who claim to be his disciples fail to sacrifice illusory wealth to redeem lives? How then could they ever attain Buddhahood?

Question: The teachings of the Catholic faith claim that the souls of animals differ from those of humans; they assert that while the human soul does not perish after death, the animal soul perishes immediately upon death.
Therefore, they say there is no karmic retribution for slaughtering them at will. What do you say to this? Answer: All things possessing blood and breath share the same fundamental nature.
Since this nature is inherently non-dual, how could their substance be different from that of humans? Thus, [the desires for] food, drink, sex, and procreation...
Their desire for life and their dread of death are exactly the same as those of humans; it is only because their physical forms are produced by the influence of karma that they differ.
How can one claim that the soul differs based on the difference in physical form? Someone might say: "Humans are able to reason while birds and beasts cannot;
therefore, we know their souls differ from those of humans. [One might also cite] that the *jiǎoduān* (unicorn) can speak and the primordial tortoise appeared [to manifest omens].

The myriad spirits, dragon-protectors of the Dharma, and the flock of cranes who heard the sutra—all were animals, yet they possessed such intelligence and spiritual power that they surpassed those of the human realm.
On what basis can one claim that the *hun* soul is inferior to humans and must suddenly perish?
That it cannot be exactly like a human being is due to the obstruction of its dark karma (*kṛṣṇa-karma*). Furthermore, our Buddha...

The precept against killing does not concern itself solely with whether the creature is destroyed; rather, one observes its suffering and pain, and the compassionate heart finds it naturally unbearable.
If even a gentleman cannot bear to pluck a blade of grass or a branch while it is still growing, how much less could he bear to harm that which possesses blood and breath?
Those who propagate such arguments are surely Western devils who have incited these heretical doctrines to indulge their own predatory cruelty.
[It is] merely that. [Question: "In this region, vegetables abound; one can avoid killing living beings there.

But for the common people living by the seashores or on the borders, who eat oxen, sheep, fish, and shrimp every day, how can they be restrained? [Answer: "Those born now in these borderlands are of low station."
This person is one who, in a previous life, committed evil and lacked faith in the Triple Gem; having created much karma through killing, they are certain to enter the three miserable realms.
If they can recognize their faults, change their ways, recite the Buddha’s name, and repent, they may perhaps avoid future calamities.

If it is impossible for them to change, then at least every morning they should prostrate to the Buddha, recite his name, or maintain the recitation of sutras and mantras, wishing that [the deceased] each day...

May all those living beings who were killed, by the power of the Buddha, swiftly attain rebirth; through their utmost sincerity and fervent lamentation, and by practicing with tireless diligence, their karmic retribution may be extinguished, and they shall be reborn in a favorable realm.

Question: The sutra states that when sentient beings eat meat, there is not one who was not their relative; many are startled by this and do not believe it, asking, "Since sentient beings are so numerous, how could it be certain that all those eaten were relatives?
Answer: Since beginningless time, sentient beings have transmigrated through the six realms of existence without rest.
As they cast off one body and take up another, they have filled the entire earth. How could this be?
If every single sentient being is a relative, then since all are indeed relatives, there is no meat being eaten now that is not from a relative;
why, then, should one have any doubt? Question:

Humans are noble and things are base; yet when it comes to killing the life of even a single creature, why does the Buddha speak so extremely of its great evil? Answer: It is because sentient beings...
Life is that which is most precious, and since slaughter is the most惨烈 (cānliè) thing in the world, its evil is the greatest.

Furthermore, when a person gives rise to a single thought of the intent to kill, it perfumes the field of the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), becoming a seed for wandering in saṃsāra through eternal kalpas.
When a sentient being who has been killed gives rise to a single thought of resentment, it likewise perfumes the field of the eighth consciousness.
In the interim, these acts become seeds of enmity and resentment accumulated over kalpas; through the convergence of causes and conditions from life to life, they will inevitably seek retribution.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If, in the interim, one takes another's life or eats their flesh, for as many kalpas as there are motes of dust, they shall devour and slaughter one another, revolving like a wheel, alternating between high and low status without rest."
Alas! How can one not be cautious? Question:
Heaven created birds and beasts for the purpose of nourishing humanity. Answer: An ancient said, "Does Heaven create meat for wolves and jackals, or humans for mosquitoes and gadflies?
It is simply that among beings and things, each consumes the other according to the strength or weakness of their respective karmic forces.
To kill one another is to bring suffering upon oneself; it is not sent by Heaven that things are thus.
It is asked: "Does one who kills domestic animals exempt those creatures from the suffering of the animal realm and cause them to transcend rebirth as human beings?"

Answer: These are the words of a demonic heretic. If an animal’s retribution for suffering has not yet been exhausted when it meets its death, it cannot escape being reborn as an animal again to undergo the suffering of slaughter once more;

if its retribution were exhausted, it would die naturally without waiting to be killed, such as when pigs and sheep die from disease. In the past, there was a man who killed many creatures on account of a marriage.

While undergoing execution, he died and entered the underworld, where he saw pigs, sheep, and other animals pleading their grievances, saying: "We committed evil deeds and fell into the realm of animals;

though our retribution is not yet exhausted, we have been unjustly slaughtered. Now we cannot avoid becoming animals once more, which will cause us to suffer the pain of the butcher's knife and block again.
The man was struck with great fear and made a vow to offer the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* as a gift.
Five thousand scrolls were provided to enable their transcendence to rebirth; in an instant, the pigs, sheep, and others all attained liberation.

The official of the underworld raised his hands and said, "The multitude of karmic creditors have all been enabled to transcend to rebirth through the power of these scriptures. The man revived as he had wished, and he printed the scriptures to distribute them (from the *Jinguangming jing ganying zhuan*).

Question: The categories of sentient beings are exceedingly vast; now, having released but a few eels and leeches, or a few hundred snails and clams, how can this be considered sufficient for compassion?
Answer: All wriggling and breathing creatures possess Buddha-nature. Viewed with the eyes of worldly convention, they may appear to be most minute things;
yet viewed with the eyes of a Buddha, they are all equally the children of the Buddha. If one rescues them...
To save the life of a single sentient being is to rescue a single Buddha-child; all the Buddhas of the ten directions will rejoice in this.

Furthermore, when the beings one rescues pass from death to life, they will surely experience great joy, which permeates the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) to serve as a cause for eternal joy throughout ten thousand kalpas.
When I give rise to a single thought of compassion and a mind of protection, it likewise permeates the storehouse consciousness.

Tian Yong has become a seed of compassion for ten thousand kalpas; even if he saves the life of but a single creature, he already possesses these two kinds of vast merit—how much more so when he saves the lives of many creatures?
Question: If all people refrain from killing, then beasts such as jackals, wolves, tigers, and leopards will fill the world;
since their ferocity and violence are even more extreme than those of humans, and they will surely devour people if not killed, how can one teach people not to kill?

The answer is: The Buddha said that if a person is endowed with the merit of a compassionate heart, no weapons, water, or fire can injure them, and no ferocious beasts or venomous insects can harm them.
It is because one possesses the ultimate compassion in the world that one can transform the ultimate violence in the world.
Formerly, during the time of Emperor Guangwu of the Han dynasty, there were many tigers in Hongnong, and the Grand Administrator and the Magistrate [were concerned].

The people set pitfall traps and prepared bows and crossbows to deal with the tiger menace, which became even more severe. When Liu Kun became the Governor, he remarked, "This is caused by oppressive government.
He ordered the people to fill in the pits and dismantle the bows and crossbows, devoting himself solely to practicing benevolent rule and showing compassion for the people;
consequently, the tigers crossed the river and departed. Although Liu Kun was not one who had attained the Way, [his actions were effective].
A single thought of benevolence can thus move even a tiger; how much more so for one who studies the compassion of the Buddha?

This is because humans are the masters of all creatures; if those who are cruel, violent, and fierce could all be transformed into beings of compassion, then poisonous and predatory creatures would likewise be transformed into auspicious phoenixes and qilin.
This is the inevitable principle of spiritual resonance (*yinggan*); it is only a matter of concern.
People lack compassion because they do not grieve over the fact that living beings do not become *qilin* or *fenghuang*.
[Someone] asks: "If one must offer sacrifices to all deities who subsist on blood, how can one perform these sacrifices without killing living beings? The answer is:
The Buddha said that by creating causes of goodness one obtains blessings, and by creating causes of killing one incurs transgressions; yet the foolish do not apply themselves to this.
To perform good deeds while making a point of killing living beings for sacrifices to exhaust one's blessings upon the deities not only fails to secure blessings but, on the contrary, incurs sin.

Moreover, if those who sacrifice to the deities can provide vegetarian offerings and recite sutras for them with dedication and transfer of merit, both the deities and themselves will obtain wholesome blessings;
why then must one kill living beings before performing a sacrifice?
Question: If one has the intention to release living beings, this is attachment to signs (*nimitta*). To neither kill nor release anything, being entirely without mind—only this accords with the Way.
Answer: These are the words of heterodox teachers; they are what the Buddha’s school calls "unspecified emptiness" (*avyākṛta-śūnyatā*).
Buddhism teaches people to give rise to the power of great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*) to rescue sentient beings from suffering. If one lacks the power of great vows, then all benefits [will be lost].
The welfare of sentient beings cannot be accomplished at all [in that way]. Formerly, King Baowen Minzhong for seven generations refrained from killing and was fond of releasing captive creatures.
When Minzhong developed heterodox views, someone instructed him, saying: "It is wondrous to neither kill nor release, entrusting oneself to a state of non-mind;
one need not cling to external forms. Minzhong gave rise to doubt and thereupon questioned Master Fahua of Chan.
He immediately rebuked him in a stern voice, saying, "Sir, you have made a great error; how can you fall into such empty views?
These wooden figures before you are all without mind—how could a few pieces of wood save suffering sentient beings? You must quickly repent for the sin of your heterodox views!
Minzhong was startled and ashamed, and he renewed his resolve to release a million lives. During a year of famine, he encountered some clams.
He exchanged several dozen hu of clams entirely for millet, recited sutras and mantras, and cast them into the middle of the stream.
That night, he dreamed that Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva appeared in a golden body to comfort and console him, saying: "I recall that in a past kalpa, I too was once born among clams;
I only urge you to firm your resolve to save sentient beings from their suffering. Thereupon, Min Zhong developed great faith and wonder, and subsequently composed [this account].

Why is it that you do not prioritize the task of loving the people first, but instead prioritize the task of loving all things? Answer: Benevolence toward the people is easy; loving all things is difficult. There may be those who can love the people but do not love all things, but there has never been anyone who loves all things without first loving the people. Therefore, I have placed the love of all things first. This is because if one does not love all things, one cannot be called a sage; yet if one does not love the people, one cannot even be called a man. Thus, I have placed the love of all things first. There are those who love things but do not love people; thus, the Bodhisattva of the *Avataṃsaka* said:

"I cannot even bear to cause suffering to a single ant, let alone to a human being. King Tang of Shang extended his heart that pushed aside the hunting net to all people, and thus his benevolence covered the world.
Formerly, when King Zhongshan was hunting, he captured a young fawn alive; his charioteer—
Baxi felt pity for it and released it, whereupon the King grew angry and banished Baxi.

Later, however, he realized: "If Baxi could not bear to harm a fawn, how could he bear to harm my own son? He appointed him as the tutor to his crown prince. When the King ascended the throne, he employed Baxi as Prime Minister;
he practiced benevolent governance with great vigor, and the entire state was brought to great order. Who would say that those who cherish all creatures are incapable of governing?
"How affectionate you are!
I ask: does the merit of giving to the poor and constructing bridges and roads not surpass that of releasing several hundred birds, fish, eels, and loaches?
He replied, "Cause and effect each respond according to their kind; through giving, one obtains the retribution of wealth and abundance."
By not killing, one obtains the retribution of long life; even if one extensively cultivates ten thousand blessings, if one does not cease the taking of life,

then although one may attain wealth and status in future lives, one will surely suffer from a short lifespan and premature death, and will be beset by many illnesses such that one cannot enjoy one's good fortune.

Question: One asks the Buddha, "Those who are prone to killing must surely receive the retribution of a short lifespan; yet why is it that in this present life there may be those who kill frequently and yet live long?

Answer: The Buddha says, "There are two kinds of karmic retribution for good and evil: first, *vipāka-phala* (fruition-retribution), which means that by performing good or evil deeds in this life, one receives the retribution of suffering or happiness in a future life; second, *pūrvanimitta-phala* (flower-retribution), which refers to [the results] in this very life."

Good and evil karma may bring the retribution of suffering or joy in this very life. If someone currently delights in killing yet enjoys longevity, it is because the merit of their previous lives was so thick that it has not yet been exhausted;
thus, they have temporarily escaped the "flower-retribution" (the immediate karmic fruit). But how could they possibly avoid the "fruit-retribution" in the three miserable realms?
Question: Can one attain Buddhahood by practicing the release of living beings with diligent effort? Answer: The *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna* states:
"If one causes sentient beings to rejoice, then one causes all Tathāgatas to rejoice. Why is this?

Because the great compassionate mind (*mahākaruṇā-citta*) constitutes the very essence of all Buddha-Tathāgatas; it is because of sentient beings that great compassion arises, and because of great compassion..."
Compassion gives rise to the bodhicitta; through the bodhicitta, one attains equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Sentient beings are the most beloved to the Buddhas as much as their own bodies and lives are to them. To save the bodies and lives of sentient beings is to fulfill the aspiration of the Tathāgatas.
During his stage of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), the Tathāgata was once the son of the Elder Jalavāhana, who saved ten thousand fish and subsequently preached the Dharma for them.

Because the fish that were mindful of the Dharma were all reborn in the heavens, and the elder’s son ultimately attained the fruit of Buddhahood, we know that the causal conditions of releasing living beings will certainly lead to Buddhahood; this cannot be compared with any other minor acts of merit.
Question: When worldly people cultivate merit by observing the fast, once the ceremony is concluded, they immediately slaughter living beings to break the fast.
Does this not nullify their merit? Answer: One who observes the fast does so with a mind of compassion as their merit.
If one intentionally slaughters living beings to break the fast, one destroys the merit of a compassionate heart and will receive the retribution of great sin. — Han Shan Zi.
A poem says: "Yesterday one was just setting up a vegetarian feast; this morning one slaughters six domestic animals. One time one builds a heaven, a hundred times one builds a hell.

This speaks of how, when the goodness of one's vegetarian practice has not yet reached even one part, the evil karma of killing has already reached a full hundred parts—just as the Buddhist sutras say:
"When passion is great and wisdom small, one flows into the ranks of the fur-bearing beasts and receives the retribution of being slaughtered."
Question: Regarding the Buddha’s teaching that those who kill living beings and eat their flesh will inevitably fall into the realms of other species, how do we know this is necessarily so? Answer:
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that "all things are created solely by the mind. Therefore, one knows that every thought-moment consists of the practice of compassion, wisdom, and vows.

If a bodhisattva, in every thought-moment, upholds the precepts, cultivates goodness, and creates the body of a human or a celestial being, yet in every thought-moment kills living beings and eats their flesh, they create the bodies of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
As the *Monthly Ordinances* (*Yueling*) states: "A yellow swallow enters the water and transforms into a clam;
because its thoughts are constantly greedy for clams as food, its form changes according to its mind, and without realizing it, it falls into the water and transforms into a clam."

All of these are matters observable in the Confucian classics. Hong Mai, the Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat, stated that he personally witnessed a pig-slaughterer who, at the moment of death, lay on the ground and let out the cry of a pig.
The ancients said that those of extreme lustfulness transform into women, while those of extreme violence transform into tigers.
Chengzi (Cheng Yi) stated that he personally saw a village dweller transform into a tiger, which then led him into his own house to devour him.
Regarding these pigs, such instances have been numerous throughout antiquity and the present; thus we know that the Buddha’s words are trustworthy and corroborated by evidence.
Humans and other species are fundamentally identical in their Buddha-nature; the reason humans differ from birds and beasts lies solely in their physical form and their mental state.
If a human lacks compassion and is capable only of killing and eating meat, they are truly nothing more than a wolf, a jackal, or a bird of prey.
As for human beings, why wait for them to be seen in a future life?
[An opponent] asks: "If the meat on that cutting board was not killed by me, but was eaten by me, what further sin is there? The answer is:
"Even if it was not killed by me, merely eating its flesh constitutes a causal condition for the killing. A former master said: "One day one should observe the fast and abstain from eating."
Regarding meat, as for the karmic act of killing committed by the people of the four continents, I have no share in it.
If there were no one to buy the meat, the butcher would likewise not kill. The butcher acts as the cause (*hetu*) of the killing and the buyer acts as the condition (*pratyaya*);

only when cause and condition are fully present is the karmic act of killing completed. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "For the sake of profit, they kill sentient beings; with wealth, they ensnare various meats."
Both are evil karmas that lead to death and falling into the Raurava Hell;

even according to the Vinaya, it does not permit bhikṣus to wear leather, silk, or fine cloth, let alone eat meat. However, because causes and conditions vary in weight, the retribution received also varies in weight.
For example, in the secular world, although crimes such as murder are divided into principal and accessory offenses, their imprisonment is uniform.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If one neither wears nor eats [the products of] the two paths of body and mind, I declare that such a person is one who has attained direct liberation.
Question: The sūtra says that observing the fast for a single day provides provisions for six hundred thousand years and brings five blessings:
first, little illness; second, physical ease; third, little lust; fourth, little sleep; and fifth, rebirth in heaven with clear consciousness.
Question: Why is it that the merit of observing the fast for even a single day according to one’s past lives is so great?
Answer: The Buddha said that the merit of a compassionate mind is the greatest. When one observes the fast for a day, one maintains a compassionate mind for that entire day;
therefore, the retribution obtained is exceedingly vast—how much more so for a long-term fast! As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Observe the seeds planted by all sentient beings..."

The seed is exceedingly minute, yet the fruit obtained is exceedingly great; as one sows a single grain in spring and reaps ten thousand ears in autumn, so too are the causes and effects of good and evil.
Thus we know that giving rise to a single thought of compassion is the root of merit for constant happiness throughout ten thousand kalpas, let alone when such thoughts continue in succession.
Question: Regarding the practice of releasing living beings to redeem their lives, those who possess wealth and means may do so; what should be done by those who lack such means? Answer:
The hearts and customs of the people of wealthy and noble families are bound together; once they take an action, the multitude joyfully follows.

If one can extensively carry out acts of redemption and greatly revitalize the wind of compassion, it is truly possible to transform customs and change social mores. As for those who certainly lack financial means...
While it is difficult to redeem life through material means, one should instead constantly make great vows and extensively engage in exhortation and transformation.

There may be those who do not require ransom with wealth and can be preserved through skillful means; furthermore, if one sees others releasing living beings, to rejoice in and praise their act brings equally great benefit.
Regarding the precept against killing:
Wang Xi zhi, the Governor of Wuxing during the Song dynasty, was fundamentally a non-believer in Buddhism. He delighted in hosting guests and devoted himself solely to slaughtering animals.

When he first served as a Langzhong (Court Gentleman) in the Western Secretariat of the Jin dynasty, he kept a pair of geese in a cage before his residence. One night, he suddenly dreamed that the mouths of the geese were emitting [light].
He took up a scroll of scripture and examined it; it entirely described matters concerning the retribution of sins and blessings. The following morning, he indeed found this very scripture.
Because of this, he never again slaughtered animals.
He of Tang, named He Ze, was a native of Rongzhou. He once served as the Acting Magistrate of Sihui in Guangzhou and raised hundreds and thousands of chickens and ducks.
In the village of Jia Pengsha, there was a man who cherished his only son exceedingly. One day, intending to cook two roosters, he set the cauldron on the fire and waited for the water to boil.
Suddenly, it seemed as though a spirit had seized his son and placed him into the pot; when he hurriedly pulled him out, both the boy and the two roosters were already cooked to a pulp.
The three brothers of Wang Zun of the Tang dynasty were all simultaneously afflicted with severe illness. In their residence there was a magpie’s nest, which chirped and cawed from dawn until dusk;
because of its clamor, the brothers collectively detested it. When they recovered from their illness, they set a snare for the magpies, cut out their tongues, and released them.
Shortly thereafter, all the brothers suffered from ailments of the mouth and teeth that no medicine could cure, and their family gradually fell into poverty.
He went out begging.

Li Ji was fond of killing living beings and skilled at archery; while his father was serving as the Governor of Bazhou, Ji set nets in the garden of the official residence and climbed to the upper story of the tower to watch for them.
Suddenly, seeing a flock of crows strike the net, Ji was so delighted that he did not even wait to put on his shoes, but rushed down barefoot to the spot.
He was wounded by a "great piercing" (juci) and heard a voice from the air saying: "Your original lifespan was long, but it has now been exhausted by your taking of life;
only a month or so remains. He subsequently died.
In Pei State, there was a scholar who had three sons; all were in their early twenties, yet they could only make sounds with their mouths and were unable to speak.
Suddenly, someone passed by the gate and asked, "Consider this for a moment: how did this come to pass?
The host reflected for a long while and said, "In the past, there were three fledglings in a swallow's nest. Their mother went out and fed them with three thorns.
Soon after, they all died. I truly regret this now. The visitor replied, "That is it."
During the Later Han dynasty, Yang Bao was seven years old when he went to Mount Hua and saw a yellow swallow that had been wounded and trapped by ants.
Moved by pity, he took it home in his headcloth box and gathered yellow flowers to feed it; after ten days, the bird was healed, and he released it.
Suddenly one morning, he dreamed of a gentleman dressed in yellow who presented him with two jade rings and said to him, "This shall cause your lineage to produce three dukes for generations."
Gong lived to the age of ninety-three; hereafter, all [the accounts] correspond.
During the Liang dynasty, there was an old woman living alone who was weaving. Suddenly, a tiger burst in and raised its paw toward her. The woman was terrified and at a loss for what to do;
seeing that the tiger appeared as if seeking rescue, she suspected it had been wounded by a thorn, and so she grasped it with her hand.
It was sufficient to pry it out with a awl, and the tiger departed more than a month later. A sack arrived as a token of gratitude, containing several ingots of white silver.
During the Taihe era, when the kitchen of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices was about to slaughter an ox, the butcher raised his blade and stepped forward, whereupon the ox knelt down.
He prostrated himself and refused to rise, and they eventually killed him. Shortly thereafter, the butcher suddenly began running about wildly, losing his normal composure;
every day he bellowed like an ox and ate only a small amount of grass. He would enter the mud and water, striking objects with his head, until after a long time he died.
During the Xianqing era of the Tang dynasty, a new bride at a shop by the roadside gave birth to a son. On the day the month was complete, her relatives held a celebratory banquet.
They intended to slaughter a sheep, but the animal repeatedly knelt and bowed toward the woman. Disregarding this, they killed it anyway.

Taking the meat to the cauldron, the woman watched as it cooked while holding her child; suddenly, the cauldron burst, and the boiling broth surged upward, striking the mother directly with ash and fire.
Both father and son died.
At the beginning of the Chongxi era, at the entrance to Mount Jing in Taizhou, there was a butcher named Zhao Ni whose family had made a profession of slaughtering pigs for generations.
One night, he suddenly dreamed that a thousand pigs spoke in human voices, saying, "We have been slaughtered and have endured nothing but suffering."
"Now your sinful karma has reached its full measure; you must depart quickly. The next day, as he was about to slaughter a pig, it suddenly cried out, went mad, and died.
There was a man from Shu named Li Shao who was fond of eating dogs and had previously killed a great many. Once, he obtained a black dog, and because of this, Li Shao...
One night, after he had returned drunk, his dog barked and howled at him. Enraged, Shao took an axe and struck the dog;

his son came out from inside, and the axe struck him squarely on the head, killing him instantly. The dog ran away, its whereabouts unknown, and Shao himself fell ill and died with the howling of a dog.

Xu Kefan, an eunuch of the Tang dynasty, was by nature fond of donkeys. He would tether a donkey in a single room, subject it to intense heat until it became distressed and thirsty, and then force-feed it a broth seasoned with the five flavors before taking its flesh as a meal. Later, while accompanying Emperor Xizong on his journey to Shu, he fell ill;
whenever he slept, he saw the donkey devouring his own flesh, and he also took pleasure in spreading fires beneath his bed to warm himself.
After pouring oil and vinegar over his body, he died shortly thereafter.
Zhao Jianmiao, a resident of Jiankang who suffered from a chronic ailment, was advised by someone that consuming deer blood would cure him.
Zhao purchased three or four deer and tied one up each day, inserting an iron tube between its flesh to extract the blood. The deer...
Zhao suffered this agony daily until strange sores broke out over his entire body; the itching was so intense that he poured boiling water from a bamboo tube onto them, and he died after two months.
At that time, someone from Dongyu in Linchuan entered the mountains and found a baby monkey; he brought it home, and the mother followed him to his house. The man bound [the monkey].
The young monkey showed itself from atop the tree; its mother beat her cheeks and piteously entreated the man, but he ultimately could not release it.

He bound and killed it, whereupon the mother-monkey wailed in grief and died. When she was dissected, her intestines were found to be completely severed. Shortly thereafter, the entire family perished from an epidemic.
During the Song dynasty, there was a monk who was habitually unscrupulous. He placed yellow atractylodes (huangjing) in a dry well and lured people in by promising it to them;
he then covered the opening with a millstone. The man inside was terrified and at his wit’s end when suddenly a fox appeared at the edge of the well and said:
"You must gaze intently at the hole in the millstone, and you may fly out. In the past, I was captured by a hunter and relied upon you to save my life; I have come now to repay your kindness."

Following his words, the benefactor indeed went out. During the Jingping era of the Song dynasty, there was a great flood in Dongyang. Cai Xifu of Yongkang took refuge on the southern ridge; at night, a large rat swam across the water and settled on the corner of his servant’s bed. The servant felt pity for it and fed it with rice. When the floodwaters receded, [the rat] followed him home. One day, while Cai Xifu was eating, the rat suddenly appeared and gnawed through the rope binding his food basket. Cai Xifu was startled and asked, "What creature is this? His wife replied, "It must be the rat that came from the flood. He then killed it and ate it. Afterward, he fell ill and died. His son, who had been away, returned and saw the bones of the rat in the kitchen. He realized it was the very one that had saved his father's life, and he wept bitterly. He buried the bones and erected a small shrine. Later, when he went to the marketplace, he encountered a man selling a rat. He recognized it as the same one and bought it. Upon returning, he prepared a meal for his family and set the rat down before them. Suddenly, the rat leaped onto the table and gnawed through the rope of the food basket. Cai Xifu was again startled and said, "This is surely the rat that saved my father's life. He killed it and ate it. That night, he dreamed of a man who said, "I am your father. Tui Xi returned to his former residence. A rat came forward with its forepaws, carrying a green pouch; inside the pouch was a large pearl, which it left placed before the bed of the slave and then departed.
On his way from the State of Sui to the State of Qi, Shou Hou saw a snake distressed in the sandy desert, with blood flowing from its head; he prodded it with a staff.
He cast them into the water and departed. Later, he went to where the snake was; the snake held one pearl toward him, but he did not dare to take it.
That night, he dreamed that his foot stepped upon a snake; startled awake, he found two pearls.
Liu Zhiheng of the Liang dynasty served as an official in Nanjun. He once dreamed that two men surnamed Li came to him begging for their lives;
Zhiheng did not understand their meaning. When morning came, he found two live carp left for him. Zhiheng said, "This must be a response to my dream," and so he released them.
That evening, he dreamed that the two men came to thank him, saying, "We shall cause you to extend your life by twelve years."
During the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty, there was a villager in Yuzhou who drained a lake to catch fish and turtles in great numbers.

He sliced off their flesh, loaded it onto wooden planks, and transported it to Jiangling to sell for a large profit in gold and silk. Upon returning home, he suddenly broke out in sores all over his body;
the pain was unbearable, and he threw his entire body into the water. Gradually, he transformed into the shape of a turtle, and after a year, his flesh rotted away and he died.
In the eighth year of the Tiānbǎo era, there was a man in Dāngtú who made his living exclusively by catching *shān* fish. That autumn, he caught three *shān* fish;
his son removed their heads and skins, lit a fire, and was about to stew them when they all turned back to look at him, transformed into snakes, and departed.
The son subsequently fell ill and died the following day. All seven members of the family died one after another until none remained.
The people of Xiuzhou were fond of eating dried eels, and one named Chen Wu had the finest stock for sale; people vied with one another to purchase them.
Later, he fell ill and lay tossing about on his bed in agony for ten days until his entire body became festering and putrid.
His wife then said that the method her husband used to prepare eels during his lifetime was extremely cruel, and that his current illness was exactly like the moment an eel dies.
Li Jian of the Tang dynasty sought out flavors extensively throughout his life. Whenever he ate a soft-shelled turtle, he would invariably bind its feet and expose it to the scorching midday sun.
Once the turtle was parched with thirst, he would give it wine and then slowly cook it.

One day, just as the turtle was about to extend its head, it suddenly lost its strength and fell to the ground, saying, "A multitude of turtles are searching for me with great urgency! Thereupon, Li Jian passed away. Shortly thereafter, Li Jian’s cook also died.
The mother of Assistant Instructor Sha, a physician in Huzhou, was fond of eating crabs and had killed countless numbers.
She died in the seventeenth year of the Shaoxing era. A ten-year-old grandson suddenly saw his grandmother break through the gate, her entire body covered in blood.
She said to the boy, "Because of my addiction to eating crabs, I have now been driven into the Crab Mountains to undergo retribution. You must print the *Shengshen Zhang* for me and burn it."
When he had finished speaking, he vanished from sight.

In Jianye during the Song dynasty, there was a woman who had a tumor growing on her back as large as a peck-measure (*dou*). Inside it were numerous objects like cocoons that made a sound whenever she walked;
she could not bear the pain and went about begging in the marketplace, saying that throughout her life she had been most fond of raising silkworms.
Because she had shared the rearing of the silkworms with her sisters-in-law, she secretly took a bag of their cocoons and burned them;
shortly thereafter, her back was afflicted with sores that gradually developed into this carbuncle, and after several years, the carbuncle burst and she died.

Lu Xiaozheng of Yongzhou during the Tang dynasty served as an assistant official in the prefectural administration of Xizhou. He was volatile by nature and committed many acts of cruelty and destruction.
Previously, there had been a hive of honeybees within the prefecture; they took flight and gathered upon a tree to the south.

Xiaozheng sent men to relocate them to another hive, but before the bees had departed, Xiaozheng grew angry and ordered that they be doused with boiling water to death. The following year, a bee suddenly stung him.
His tongue became red and swollen, blocking his mouth, and he died.
At Daci Temple in Shu Commandery, there was a Vinaya Master named Xiuzhun whose character was extremely narrow and irritable. He had planted bamboo in front of his courtyard;
many ants crawled up the railings from them. Xiuzhun grew angry and cut down all the bamboo, catching the ants and throwing them into a fire of ashes. Later, Xiuzhun...
Suddenly, he suffered from sores covering his entire body and face. A physician said, "This is 'ant-leak' sores (yichou-chuang); it cannot be cured," and later he indeed died.
At Jinhuasi Temple in Shu Commandery, Master Xiurong had many pine and cypress trees in his courtyard that were infested with countless hairy insects.
Xiurong became enraged and ordered his men to clear them away, mixing them with firewood and piling them in the scorching sun to dry them to death. After more than a month, they were exposed.
Suddenly, tens of thousands of insects appeared and bit his body before departing.
Emperor Wenzong of the Tang dynasty was fond of clams; one day there was a clam that would not open. The Emperor opened it himself, and inside was an image of Avalokiteśvara.
Startled and amazed, he summoned Chan Master Weizheng to inquire about it. The Master replied, "It is to awaken Your Majesty’s faith."
The *Ārya-śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "To those who are to be saved by the body of a bodhisattva, one manifests the body of a bodhisattva and preaches the Dharma for them.

The Emperor said, "I have seen the bodhisattva body, but I have not heard the preaching of the Dharma. The Master replied, "Does Your Majesty believe this? The Emperor said, "How could I dare not believe it?
The Master said, "I shall preach the Dharma for Your Majesty. When he had finished preaching, the Emperor was greatly delighted and subsequently abstained from food.
The Emperor Hagi issued an edict establishing an Avalokiteśvara image.

Postscript to the *Jingci Yaoyu*.
Jingci is a renowned monastery where Great Master Wengu established his hermitage when he traveled to Jianzhou; it was there that he first initiated his work of guiding both monastics and laypeople,
and thus [this place] was entrusted to him.
Master Yongjue composed over twenty thousand words of essential sayings to broaden the milk of the Dharma;
this was truly a continuation of the illustrious legacy of Master Yunqi.
Master Yunqi established the eight pillars of correct discipline to guide our fourfold assembly, while Master Yongjue took up the two robes at the head of the path to initiate its beginning.

The practice of spreading mats at the gates and performing vigorous exhortations has been established for many years; thus, it is known by every household south of the Great River and has become a customary tradition.

How could its benefit be considered slight? In recent years, while the *chānqīng* (comets) have not yet subsided and the regions between Qin and Chu have seen smoke from fires darken the day and the glow of phosphorescent flames turn the night green, only Jiangnan alone has remained peaceful.

The Imperial benevolence has reached even the most obscure dwellings, such that the whistling arrows have ceased and all alarms are hushed; could this not be due to the power of the Dharma’s subtle assistance?
Now, the Great Master Yongjue has moved his staff to Zhenji Temple to succeed me.

Having heard the sound of the Master’s Dharma wheel, which flows like clouds from the ocean of the Tripiṭaka and expands the Brahma-net throughout the forest of *cāṇa* trees, I shall once again brandish the fly-whisk and let the thunder of the Dharma resound.
Thus, may the eight directions and the seven assemblies of followers alike ascend to the realm of purity, benevolence, and longevity.
